title: config.json and jobs.json are written non-atomically, and corrupt-load recovery destroys the last-good .bak within seconds — one torn write permanently wipes all presets, environments, and job definitions
existing_state: The two highest-value files bypass the project's own atomic writer. ConfigurationService.Save writes config.json — which holds ALL presets/scripts, environments, host lists, and the compressed ApplicationState blob — with a plain File.WriteAllText (Services/ConfigurationService.cs:144) after a best-effort .bak copy with an empty catch (ConfigurationService.cs:116-120); JobStorageService.PersistToDisk writes jobs.json the same way (Services/JobStorageService.cs:243, .bak copy at :230-233). Utilities/JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic (JsonFileWriter.cs:21-88, temp file + File.Replace) exists and is used by both history stores (JobHistoryService.cs:227,425; HistoryStorageService.cs:739-740), and CLAUDE.md names it as the convention. Exposure is constant: config saves fire on every Update()/settings change and app close (ConfigurationService.cs:156-161; Form1.cs:3947), and jobs.json is rewritten TWICE per scheduled run for RunningState bookkeeping (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:768-774, 827-832). Worse, recovery cascades into total loss: on a corrupt load, ConfigurationService.Load COPIES the bad file to .corrupt (TryBackupCorrupt default useMove:false, Utilities/JsonFileWriter.cs:103-117), leaves the corrupt config.json in place, never attempts .bak, and returns defaults (ConfigurationService.cs:91-102). The very next Save() copies the still-corrupt on-disk file OVER the good config.json.bak (ConfigurationService.cs:116-120) before writing defaults — and that save is guaranteed within seconds because the silent startup update check writes LastCheckTime via _configService.Update (Form1.cs:439-441, 14983; CheckOnStartup defaults true at Models/AppConfiguration.cs:457), or at latest at app close. After one corruption event plus one save: live file = defaults, .bak = corrupt, .corrupt = corrupt. JobStorageService has the identical cascade (TryBackupCorrupt copy at JobStorageService.cs:92, .bak clobber at :230-233, empty job roster at :95-97, no .bak fallback in Load at :65-99). The warning dialog (Form1.cs:350-354) mentions only .corrupt, never the good .bak, and offers no restore. Compounding the jobs.json exposure, the scheduler's Saves run on ThreadPool threads against the unsynchronized plain Dictionary _jobs (JobStorageService.cs:15) while the UI thread enumerates Jobs.Values every 5 s (Form1.cs:15205, 15224) and the evaluation loop enumerates it too (JobExecutionService.cs:313): two jobs completing in the same instant collide in File.WriteAllText (IOException 'file in use') and mutate the Dictionary mid-enumeration (undefined behavior); if CompleteJob's Save throws, RunningState is never cleared, so the NEXT launch falsely reports 'Application crashed during execution' for a run that finished fine.
recommendation: Route both saves through JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic(path, json, createBackup: true) — a near drop-in replacement that subsumes the hand-rolled .bak copies and makes backup+swap atomic. In both corrupt-load paths: call TryBackupCorrupt with useMove:true (so the corrupt file can never be re-copied over .bak), then attempt to parse {path}.bak and restore from it before falling back to defaults/empty list, surfacing 'restored from backup' via ConfigLoadError/LoadError; additionally, skip the .bak refresh in Save while a load-failure flag is set. Make the Form1.cs:350-354 dialog actionable (Restore from backup (last saved <time>) / Start with defaults / Open config folder). In JobStorageService, add a private lock taken in Save/Delete/RestoreSnapshots/Load/PersistToDisk and have the Jobs property snapshot under it; optionally move RunningState out of the full jobs.json roster rewrite (sidecar file) so roster rewrites only happen on actual edits.
user_benefit: A power cut or crash during one of the app's frequent automatic saves — or two jobs finishing simultaneously — can currently wipe every saved preset, environment, host list, and scheduled-job definition beyond recovery, even though a perfect backup existed moments earlier. This closes the data-loss hole using a helper the codebase already ships.
mockup_idea: Before/after dialog mockup: current passive 'Configuration file was corrupted... defaults applied' vs a recovery dialog with 'Restore from backup (last saved 2026-06-09 18:42)' / 'Start with defaults' / 'Open config folder' buttons.

evidence.note: Save: best-effort .bak copy (116-120) then raw File.WriteAllText at :144 — truncate-then-write, non-atomic; after a corrupt load the .bak copy source is the still-corrupt file
corrupt path: COPY to .corrupt (useMove:false), corrupt config.json left in place, defaults returned, .bak never tried
plain Dictionary, corrupt->empty fallback, .bak copy at :232 then File.WriteAllText at :243, no .bak fallback in Load
WriteJsonAtomic exists and is used by the history services; TryBackupCorrupt default is COPY not MOVE
RunningState persistence rewrites jobs.json on ThreadPool threads at start and end of every scheduled run — two corruption windows per run plus concurrent-save collisions
startup update check triggers Update->Save seconds after launch (CheckOnStartup default true); warning dialog offers no restore; UI thread enumerates Jobs.Values every 5 s concurrently with writes

verification.notes: Traced every cited path; the finding is accurate. config.json and jobs.json both use raw File.WriteAllText after a best-effort .bak copy, and the corrupt-load recovery (TryBackupCorrupt copies, never moves; .bak never consulted) means the very next Save — guaranteed within seconds by the startup update check writing LastCheckTime (CheckOnStartup defaults true), or at latest on app close — copies the still-corrupt file over the only good backup. The scheduler concurrency claims also hold (jobStorage.Save on ThreadPool timer threads, no lock, UI enumerates Jobs.Values on a 5s timer; the false "crashed during execution" report follows from a throwing CompleteJob save). Only minor nuance: the dictionary mid-enumeration race needs a UI-thread job add/delete (scheduler saves only overwrite existing keys), but the cross-thread unsynchronized access and File.WriteAllText collision are real regardless. Critical severity is justified: one torn write during routine automatic saves permanently destroys all presets, environments, and job definitions despite a good backup existing moments earlier. | impact check: Traced every citation; the finding holds as written. The decisive part is verified end-to-end: after a corrupt load, TryBackupCorrupt COPIES (leaves the corrupt config.json in place), .bak is never consulted, and the very next Save — guaranteed within seconds by the unconditional LastCheckTime write after the startup update check (CheckOnStartup defaults true), or at app close — copies the corrupt file over the last-good .bak before writing defaults. So a single torn write becomes permanent loss of all presets/environments/jobs despite WriteJsonAtomic existing and being used by the sibling history services; the recommendation is sound and not implemented anywhere for these two files. One minor nuance: the scheduler's jobs-dictionary writes are existing-key overwrites, which on .NET 8 don't invalidate enumerators, so the "mutate mid-enumeration" crash is less likely in practice than implied (the concurrent File.WriteAllText IOException and false 'crashed during execution' report are real, MaxConcurrentJobs defaults to 3). Critical is justified per rubric: unrecoverable data loss with constant exposure (config saves on every settings change/close; jobs.json rewritten twice per scheduled run). All other cited lines exact.]

title: Running a preset against a vault_path host deadlocks (hangs) the entire app on the first uncached secret read
existing_state: VaultCredentialProvider.TryGetPassword resolves a vault secret by blocking on async with `_vaultService.ReadSecretKeysAsync(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult()` (Services/Vault/VaultCredentialProvider.cs:48-49). VaultService never uses ConfigureAwait(false) anywhere (grep over Services/Vault found ConfigureAwait only in VaultOidcLoginFlow.cs) — ReadSecretKeysAsync -> GetAuthenticatedProfileAsync (VaultService.cs:282-313) -> AuthenticateWith*Async -> SendWithErrorTranslationAsync all await without ConfigureAwait(false), so the first genuinely-async HTTP continuation captures the calling thread's SynchronizationContext. Form1.GetHostConnections calls TryGetPassword at Form1.cs:13334, and the main preset path ExecutePresetOnRowsAsync runs synchronously from method entry (Form1.cs:12268) to `GetHostConnections(hostRows).ToList()` (Form1.cs:12277) with NO await in between — i.e. on the WinForms UI thread, which has a WindowsFormsSynchronizationContext. When the secret is not cached (first run after launch, after the 300s CacheTtl expires, or a new path/profile), the HTTP continuation is posted back to the UI thread while the UI thread is blocked inside GetResult() -> classic sync-over-async deadlock. The app hangs permanently and must be force-killed, losing any in-progress work. (If the profile is OIDC with an expired token it is even worse: the blocking call launches a full HttpListener browser login on the UI thread.)
recommendation: Make the credential resolution off the UI thread or non-blocking. Minimal fix: add ConfigureAwait(false) to every await in VaultService (ReadSecretKeysAsync/ReadSecretAsync/GetAuthenticatedProfileAsync/SendWithErrorTranslationAsync/auth methods/KV detect) so continuations don't require the UI thread. Better: make GetHostConnections async (resolve vault_path via `await ReadSecretKeysAsync`) and await it in ExecutePresetOnRowsAsync, or hoist the vault resolution onto a Task.Run/await boundary before building HostConnection so no Vault HTTP ever runs under .GetAwaiter().GetResult() on the UI thread. Add a regression test that resolves a vault_path on a thread carrying a SynchronizationContext.
user_benefit: Users who store SSH credentials in Vault (a headline feature) can currently freeze the whole app just by clicking Run on a host whose secret isn't already cached. Fixing this keeps the app responsive and prevents lost work from force-kills.

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: TryGetPassword blocks the WinForms UI thread on GetAwaiter().GetResult() (VaultCredentialProvider.cs:48-49), VaultService has zero ConfigureAwait(false) (verified by grep), and ExecutePresetOnRowsAsync reaches GetHostConnections/TryGetPassword with no prior await from async-void UI handlers — so any uncached vault_path read (first run after launch, post-300s-TTL, new path/profile) posts its HTTP continuation to the blocked UI thread: permanent hang, force-kill required. Only nit: the OIDC aside is slightly off — an expired OIDC token deadlocks at the first auth_url HTTP await before the browser/HttpListener flow ever launches (same hang, not worse). The same blocking call is also reachable from the parallel connection-test path (Form1.cs:8916). Critical severity is justified: app-wide hang on the primary Run path for Vault-backed hosts. | impact check: Traced end-to-end and it holds: TryGetPassword blocks on GetResult (VaultCredentialProvider.cs:48-49), VaultService.cs has zero ConfigureAwait(false), and all five run entry points are async-void UI handlers reaching GetHostConnections().ToList() (Form1.cs:12277) with no prior await — so the first uncached vault read posts its HTTP continuation to the blocked UI thread: permanent deadlock, and HttpClient's timeout cannot rescue it (the fault continuation also needs the UI thread). No mitigating layer exists: the cache only fills after a successful read, and the scheduler path runs the same call safely on a background thread (likely why this went unnoticed); the connection-test path (Form1.cs:8916) shares the bug. Only nit: the OIDC parenthetical is slightly off — it deadlocks at the first HTTP continuation before any browser launches — and note ConfigureAwait(false) alone removes the deadlock but still freezes the UI for the HTTP duration, so the async-off-UI-thread option is the real fix.

title: writefile JSON append silently destroys the existing file when the merge fails
existing_state: In `writefile` with `format: json, mode: append`, FormatAsJson reads the existing file and tries to merge (Services/Scripting/Commands/WriteFileCommand.cs:217-233). If the existing content fails to parse as JSON (MergeJsonContent returns null on JsonException at :283-286), if the new value is not an object while the file holds an object (:276-277 returns null), or if the read itself throws (:229-232), execution falls through to `return SerializeToJson(newValue, ...)` at :235 — and ExecuteAsync then does `File.WriteAllText(filePath, content)` at :101, replacing the ENTIRE file with only the newest record. The only diagnostics are Debug-level messages (:231, :276, :285) and the step returns Ok. All writes are also plain non-atomic File.WriteAllText/AppendAllText (:101, :113, :118, :127, :131), so a crash/power loss mid-write leaves a torn JSON file — which then triggers exactly this destroy-on-next-append path on the following run. A multi-host preset accumulating per-host results into one JSON file can lose the whole accumulation from one bad write.
recommendation: In append mode, treat a failed merge as a step failure instead of falling through to overwrite: have MergeJsonContent failures return an error result (honoring on_error) and never rewrite the file, or at minimum rename the unparseable file to *.bak before replacing it and emit at Warning/Error level. Separately, switch the write paths to the project's own atomic convention (temp file + File.Replace, like Utilities/JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic) so a torn write can't corrupt the file in the first place.
user_benefit: Stops a script that is supposed to be appending results from wiping out everything it previously collected — the exact opposite of what the user asked for — with no visible error.

evidence.note: append-mode merge; any failure (parse error, non-object merge, read error) returns/sets null and falls through to SerializeToJson(newValue) — only the new value survives
JSON 'append' writes via File.WriteAllText — the merged-or-fallback content fully replaces the file, non-atomically
merge failures emit only ScriptOutputType.Debug and return null (the destroy trigger); step still returns Ok

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds exactly as written. In json+append mode, any merge failure (unparseable existing file, non-object appended onto an object file, read exception, or even a scalar JSON root) makes MergeJsonContent return null, FormatAsJson falls through to serializing only the new value, and ExecuteAsync's File.WriteAllText(:101) replaces the whole file — then returns CommandResult.Ok(). The "silent" part is stronger than the finding states: ScriptContext.EmitOutput (ScriptContext.cs:875) drops ALL Debug-level output unless DebugMode is on, so in a normal run there is zero visible trace. All writes are non-atomic, so the command can manufacture its own corrupt file that triggers the wipe on the next run. Cited line numbers are accurate; the recommended fixes (fail the step, .bak the file, atomic write) are not implemented anywhere in the command. | impact check: Traced and confirmed: every merge-failure path in FormatAsJson (parse error :283-285, non-object-into-object :276-277, read exception :229-232) falls through to serializing only the new value, which File.WriteAllText at :101 then writes over the entire file — with Debug-only diagnostics and a successful step result, so on_error never fires. No mitigating layer exists: no .bak, writes are non-atomic, JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic is unused here, and tests cover only JSONL/text append (the fall-through is not a tested contract). SCRIPTING.md (:2105, :5189, :6323) actively recommends the multi-host JSON-append accumulator pattern and documents only "intelligent merging", never the silent-overwrite fallback. One nuance: with the documented array-accumulator pattern a malformed NEW value is harmlessly appended as a string — total loss requires the existing file to be unparseable (torn write, hand edit, concurrent writer) or an object-file/non-object mismatch — but the command's own non-atomic writes can create exactly that torn file, and the loss is silent and unrecoverable, so critical stands.

title: Flow Canvas copy/paste keeps stale container-membership metadata — pasted blocks silently vanish from exported YAML or duplicate steps inside the original container
existing_state: Ctrl+C/Ctrl+V uses an internal clipboard that deep-copies the whole node including data.props (FlowCanvas/src/utils/clipboard.ts:44-57). It re-ids nodes and remaps edge endpoints via idMap (clipboard.ts:59-67) but never strips or remaps the structural metadata `_isChildOf`, `_stepPath`, `_membershipFromConnect`, `_forceGraphExport`, or band cosmetics; the paste site adds nodes as-is (FlowCanvas/src/hooks/useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:63-74). A pasted copy of any block that lives inside a container (most blocks in a real preset — every imported block has `_stepPath`) still points at the ORIGINAL container with the ORIGINAL index. Verified consequences: (1) On Apply, the C# exporter skips every node with `_isChildOf` from top-level emission (Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1278-1281, 'Visual-only child nodes do not emit YAML') — if the original container exports via its stored snippet, the pasted block is silently absent from the saved YAML and vanishes on next open, despite being editable and wireable on canvas. (2) If the container regenerates from graph (any prop edit walks `_forceGraphExport` up the `_isChildOf` ancestor chain), children are collected purely by `_isChildOf == containerId` + `_stepPath` (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1509-1542), so the pasted copy is emitted as a duplicate step INSIDE the original container — e.g. a duplicated `send` runs twice per loop iteration against every host, regardless of where the user placed the copy. (3) Duplicate `_stepPath` values break debug correlation: BuildStepPathToNodeMap is first-wins (Form1.cs:13713-13723), so step highlighting/output lands on the wrong copy. (4) Branch bands fold the pasted node into the original container's lane (utils/branchBands.ts:156-169) and removal-triggered renumbering treats it as a real sibling (utils/childMembership.ts:229-296). (5) The clipboard is module-level and survives `load-graph` (clipboard.ts:9; nothing in stores/messageBridge.ts clears it), and node ids are `node-{counter}` per import (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:331), so pasting after switching presets can attach the block to an unrelated container in the new preset whose id collides.
recommendation: In pasteNodes (utils/clipboard.ts), post-process each pasted node's data.props: if the `_isChildOf` target was part of the copied set, remap it through idMap (preserving copied-container subtrees); otherwise strip `_isChildOf`, `_stepPath`, `_membershipFromConnect`, `_forceGraphExport`, `_blankLinesBefore`, and the cosmetic keys (`_branchLabel`, `_branchColor`, `_depth`) — keeping `_yamlSnippet` so a pasted top-level block still round-trips its content. Sanitized pastes then behave like fresh palette drops: they export as orphan/root steps and the existing childMembership.ts onConnect path confers correct membership when wired in. Also clear the module clipboard on `load-graph` (or stamp it with a preset token) to kill the cross-preset id-collision case. Add a unit test that pastes an imported container child and asserts the exported YAML neither drops nor duplicates it and the clone carries no underscore metadata.
user_benefit: Copy/paste is the most natural way to duplicate a step; today it can silently make a fleet run execute an extra SSH command inside a loop, or silently lose the pasted block on save. Both are invisible until something runs wrong.

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and all five consequences hold: paste deep-copies _isChildOf/_stepPath unsanitized, the exporter skips such nodes at top level (silent drop when the container round-trips its snippet — and paste alone does not trip the regen detectors, so the snippet path is what runs), and on regeneration CollectBranchChain collects branch members purely by _isChildOf+_stepPath, emitting the clone as a duplicate step. It is actually slightly worse than written: editing any prop on the pasted copy walks its stale _isChildOf chain (graphSlice updateNodeProp) and force-regenerates the ORIGINAL container, so "paste then tweak the copy" immediately injects the duplicate. Severity critical stands: silent YAML data loss plus a silently duplicated command per loop iteration against every host. | impact check: Traced end-to-end: pasteNodes deep-copies props with no metadata strip, the exporter skips any `_isChildOf` node at top level (silent drop), and once the user edits the pasted copy (the whole point of duplicating) `_forceGraphExport` walks the stale ancestor chain and CollectBranchChain's metadata sweep (`_isChildOf` + immediate-child `_stepPath`) emits the clone as a duplicate step inside the original container — so paste-then-edit-then-Apply, the most natural flow, yields either a vanished or a doubly-executed SSH step with zero diagnostics. The one mitigating layer I found, the onConnect rehome seam (graphSlice.ts:382-394, targetIsOrphaned), only repairs the paste if the user wires it as the target of a membership-conferring gesture from an imported nested source; wiring it after a top-level block or a canvas-authored block (childMembership.ts:85,111 return null) leaves the stale metadata intact, and Ctrl+C/V is the app's only duplication affordance (no context-menu Duplicate exists). The recommendation is not implemented anywhere (setNodes is a plain set, no clipboard tests exist, nothing clears the module clipboard on load-graph), so critical stands. title: Per-host passwords are stored under one credential key but looked up under another — silently lost for any host using a non-default port
existing_state: When Windows Credential Manager is available, the app moves plaintext `password` cells into the credential store and blanks the cell, keyed by the RAW Host_IP cell text: on environment load (Form1.cs:2294-2303), on every environment switch and app close via BuildApplicationState (Form1.cs:14726-14747 — also writes the blank into the persisted state), on startup state restore (Form1.cs:14824-14833), and in MigratePasswordsToCredentialManager (Form1.cs:1510-1521). At execution time, however, GetHostConnections resolves the password under a DIFFERENT key: it parses Host_IP, overrides the port from the documented `port` convention column (Form1.cs:13317-13325), and looks up `host.ToString()` (Form1.cs:13346-13356), which renders `ip:port` for non-22 ports and bare `ip` for port 22 (Models/HostConnection.cs:92). So a row with Host_IP `10.0.0.5` and port column `2222` stores the password under `10.0.0.5` but looks it up under `10.0.0.5:2222` — a guaranteed miss; `host:22` in the Host_IP cell mismatches the other direction. The username half of the key has the same drift: it falls back to the live toolbar username at blank time (Form1.cs:2298) vs at run time (Form1.cs:13348), so changing the toolbar username also orphans stored passwords. On a miss the run silently falls back to the toolbar default password (Services/SshExecutionService.cs:1198, 1300) — wrong credentials fired at the whole fleet, with the grid cell already blanked so the user sees nothing to fix.
recommendation: Create one key-builder helper (parse the Host_IP cell, apply the `port` column override, return HostConnection.ToString() plus a deterministic username resolution) and use it at every StoreHostPassword/TryResolveHostPassword call site (Form1.cs:1520, 2301, 13351, 13353, 14733, 14831). At resolve time, additionally probe the legacy raw-cell key so passwords already stored under the old key are migrated forward instead of lost. Consider warning (status bar) when a per-host password lookup misses and the default password is substituted.
user_benefit: Hosts with hardened/non-default SSH ports stop silently authenticating with the wrong password after an environment switch or app restart — which today can fail whole fleet runs and even trigger account lockouts on devices that count failed logins.

every env switch/app close: same raw-key store + blanks password into persisted state

Parse/ToString normalize the key: drops :22, renders ip:port otherwise
empty host.Password silently falls back to toolbar default password

verification.notes: Traced fully and confirmed: all four blank-and-store sites key by the raw Host_IP cell text, while the run-time lookup keys by HostConnection.ToString() after the port-column override (ip:port for non-22), and CredentialTargets does no normalization — so non-22-port rows (and :22-suffixed cells, and toolbar-username changes) miss and silently fall back to the toolbar default password (SshExecutionService.cs:1198/1300). One nuance the finding omits: GetHostConnections also stores under the correct ToString() key when the password cell is still populated at run time (Form1.cs:13351), so "type → run → restart" is masked; the guaranteed loss hits passwords blanked before any run (environment load, state restore, close/env-switch without running) and password changes saved without a run — which can additionally serve a stale password from the old correctly-keyed entry. High severity is justified: wrong credentials silently fired at hosts with the evidence (the grid cell) already blanked.

title: Recurring cron jobs fire at UTC-interpreted times while every UI surface shows local-time interpretation
existing_state: The due-check for recurring jobs is IsJobDue -> SchedulingService.GetMissedOccurrences (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:1028), which calls Cronos's zone-less cron.GetOccurrences(lastCheckedUtc, DateTime.UtcNow, ...) (Services/SchedulingService.cs:97) — cron fields are matched against the UTC clock. But every place the user sees the schedule uses GetNextRunLocal, which passes TimeZoneInfo.Local to Cronos (Services/SchedulingService.cs:61) — local-clock interpretation: the status-bar countdown (Form1.cs:15230), the Job List 'Next Run' column (JobListDialog.cs:741), and the cron builder's live next-run preview (UI/CronBuilderControl.cs:622). Missed-run detection (SchedulingService.cs:126,165) also uses the UTC interpretation. On any machine not set to UTC, a job built as 'Daily at 9:00 AM' displays next-run 9:00 AM local but actually executes at 9:00 UTC (e.g. 1:00 AM PST) — display and execution disagree by the full UTC offset on every field-anchored schedule. Only pure-interval crons (*/5 * * * *) coincidentally agree. One-time schedules are unaffected (the editor converts local->UTC explicitly).
recommendation: Make execution match the displayed local-time semantics with one change: in GetMissedOccurrences (SchedulingService.cs:97), use the Cronos overload that accepts a TimeZoneInfo and pass TimeZoneInfo.Local. That single change fixes IsJobDue, DetectMissedRuns, and DetectMissedRunSummaries together since they all funnel through it. Audit GetNextRunUtc (SchedulingService.cs:71-80) callers for consistency, and add a unit test that pins a non-UTC zone and asserts a '0 9 * * *' occurrence lands at 9 AM in that zone; verify DST transition behavior (Cronos handles skipped/ambiguous times when given a zone).
user_benefit: Scheduled fleet commands actually run at the time the UI promised. Today every non-UTC user's cron jobs silently run hours off — e.g. a 'business hours' maintenance script firing in the middle of the night, or vice versa.
mockup_idea: Two-row before/after: Job List showing 'Next Run: Tomorrow 9:00 AM' next to a history row stamped 'Started 1:00 AM' (before), versus matching 9:00 AM in both (after).

Next Run column rendered from GetNextRunLocal (local interpretation)
Status-bar countdown computed from GetNextRunLocal

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the split is exactly as described: the scheduler due-check (JobExecutionService.cs:1028 -> SchedulingService.cs:97) uses Cronos's zone-less GetOccurrences, which matches cron fields against the UTC clock, while all three user-visible surfaces (Form1.cs:15230, JobListDialog.cs:741, CronBuilderControl.cs:622) are the only callers of GetNextRunLocal (SchedulingService.cs:61), which passes TimeZoneInfo.Local. No compensating conversion exists — the cron string is saved verbatim, and the only local->UTC conversion is the one-time path (JobEditorDialog.cs:2024-2025), confirming one-time jobs are unaffected. Cronos 0.11.1 (csproj line 64) has the zone-aware GetOccurrences overload, so the recommended one-line fix is valid and not yet implemented; missed-run detection (SchedulingService.cs:126,165) funnels through the same method and is fixed by it too.

title: Overdue one-time jobs auto-execute immediately at app launch, violating the 'missed runs are never auto-executed' policy
existing_state: IsJobDue treats a one-time job as due whenever OneTimeScheduleUtc <= now with no staleness bound (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:1030-1031), and the evaluation timer's first tick fires immediately at startup (Start() dueTime Zero, JobExecutionService.cs:177-181). Recurring jobs are protected from downtime catch-up by _lastEvaluationUtc being initialized to construction time (JobExecutionService.cs:93), and startup missed-run detection deliberately records-without-running — but it filters to ScheduleType.Recurring only (Services/SchedulingService.cs:120, 159), matching the documented policy 'never auto-executed' (Models/SkippedRunEntry.cs:5). Net effect: an enabled one-time job whose moment passed while the app was closed (scheduled 2 PM, app closed at 1 PM, reopened days later) executes against its whole host fleet seconds after launch — no prompt, no skipped-run record — no matter how stale the schedule is. On success it is then marked 'One-time schedule completed' (JobExecutionService.cs:877-881) as if it ran on time. Extend DetectMissedRunSummaries (or a sibling) to cover OneTime so startup detection records it, and pair it with a startup prompt so the user can consciously fire it late via Run Now. Also decide the cancelled-one-time re-fire semantics explicitly (today cancellation leaves it armed to re-fire on the next tick).
user_benefit: A maintenance script scheduled for last Tuesday's change window can currently blast the fleet the moment you open the app on Friday. Aligning one-time jobs with the existing recurring-job policy removes the most dangerous surprise in the scheduler.

title: Conditions and when: guards silently resolve typo'd/undefined variables, flipping branches with no diagnostic
existing_state: Condition evaluation resolves an unknown identifier to a value that depends on syntax, never an error. In ValueResolver.ResolveExpressionValue an undefined bare token returns the literal token string (ValueResolver.cs:288) and a `${var}`/`{{var}}` form returns empty string (ValueResolver.cs:272-273 via SubstituteVariables, which yields empty for missing vars at ScriptContext.cs:559-565,704). So `when: "${enabled} == true"` where the real column is `enable` evaluates AreEqual("", "true") = false (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:155-167,399-416) and the step is silently skipped, while bare `when: enabled` with `enabled` undefined falls through to a truthiness check of the literal string "enabled" and evaluates TRUE (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:206-207, ValueResolver.IsTruthyValue:357-359). The executor treats a skipped guard as an intentional success (ScriptExecutor.cs:348-365) and `matches` swallows regex errors returning false (ExpressionEvaluator.cs:100-103). Crucially, conditions/when:/set RHS get no parse-time validation at all — only grid columns get a pre-run warning via the dependency analyzer; a typo in a local/loop variable is invisible. The same silent-empty resolution governs `if`, `elif`, and `while`, so a misspelled variable silently takes the wrong branch (or loops zero/forever) across the whole fleet.
recommendation: Distinguish 'undefined variable' from 'empty value' in condition resolution: when a referenced identifier is neither a defined variable, a known built-in, nor a literal, surface a warning through EmitOutput (and ideally fail the step under a strict mode) instead of coercing to empty/literal. Add a parse-time lint pass that flags identifiers in conditions/when:/set RHS that are not defined vars, declared params, grid columns, or built-ins, reusing the reference-collection the ScriptDependencyAnalyzer already does.
user_benefit: A one-character typo in a condition stops silently inverting branch logic across every host; the author sees a warning instead of a run that 'worked' but did the wrong thing.

title: A failed inline vault read silently substitutes an empty string, sending blank credentials to hosts
existing_state: ResolveVaultExpression catches a failed secret read and returns `string.Empty` after only setting `_last_error` (ScriptContext.cs:751-755); the missing-configuration and missing-`#` paths do the same (ScriptContext.cs:709-713, 720-724, 740-744). Because this happens inside string interpolation (SubstituteVariables, ScriptContext.cs:769/777), there is no channel to fail the step — the surrounding `send`/`print`/`set` proceeds with the secret silently collapsed to empty. So if Vault is unreachable, the token/key is wrong, or auth lapsed, `send: "login -u admin -p{{vault:db#password}}"` transmits `login -u admin -p` with no password to every host. On network gear and SSH logins this can trigger lockouts or auth-failure storms across the fleet, and the only signal is `_last_error` which most scripts never check.
recommendation: Give inline vault failures a hard-fail path: have ResolveVaultExpression throw a dedicated exception on read/config failure and let the consuming command (send/print/set) convert it into a CommandResult.Fail so the step stops instead of sending an empty secret. At minimum, log the failure through EmitOutput at Error level rather than only writing the silent `_last_error` variable.
user_benefit: A transient Vault outage or a bad secret path fails the step loudly instead of quietly logging in with a blank password across every host, preventing account lockouts and confusing partial runs.

title: A misspelled function name in value position silently becomes the literal call text — which then gets sent to hosts or compared in conditions
existing_state: Function dispatch in value contexts falls through on unknown names instead of erroring. For `- set: cmd = uper(name)`: SetCommand tries TryEvaluateFunctionExpression (Services/Scripting/Commands/SetCommand.cs:178), which parses the call but hits the legacy switch's `default: return false` (Services/Scripting/JsonUtilities.cs:562-563); the chain then ends at ValueResolver.ResolveExpressionValue, which returns the raw expression text as a string (Services/Scripting/ValueResolver.cs:288). The variable now holds the literal string "uper(name)", and a later `- send: {{cmd}}` executes that literal on every host. The same fall-through exists in JsonUtilities.ResolveJsonValue (JsonUtilities.cs:312-333) and in inline substitution `{{uper(name)}}` via ScriptContext.ResolveVariableExpression (ScriptContext.cs:687-704). By contrast, the SAME typo inside an if:/while:/assert: condition throws FormatException("Unknown function: ...") (Services/Scripting/ExpressionParser.cs:422-437) — so the engine already knows how to fail, just inconsistently. ScriptParser performs no static validation of function names, so nothing catches this before runtime either.
recommendation: In the value-resolution chain (ValueResolver.ResolveExpressionValue and JsonUtilities.ResolveJsonValue), when TryParseFunctionCall succeeds (the expression is unambiguously a single name(...) call with an identifier name) but neither the registry, the legacy switch, nor json.* claims the name, throw the same FormatException the ExpressionParser throws instead of falling through to the literal. Additionally, add a parse-time validation warning in ScriptParser that checks called names against the union of FunctionRegistry.RegisteredNames + the legacy switch names + the json.* set, so typos surface in the editor before a fleet run.
user_benefit: A one-character typo currently changes behavior silently: garbage commands run on every host, or a condition variable holds a non-empty literal string that is always truthy. Failing at parse/eval time turns a silent fleet-wide misfire into an immediate, pinpointed error.

title: exit command silently reports Success for bare failure messages, and variable substitution can flip the exit status
existing_state: ExitCommand defaults the status to Success for any message that doesn't start with an English keyword: `exit: "Could not reach host"` produces `[EXIT Success] Could not reach host` and CommandResult.Exit(Success) (Services/Scripting/Commands/ExitCommand.cs:21-22, fall-through else at 61-64). Worse, variables are substituted BEFORE keyword parsing (line 18, parse at 24-60), so the status is derived from runtime data: `exit: "{{summary}}"` where summary happens to start with 'error ', 'fail '/'failure ', or 'success ' flips the exit status to whatever the data says — e.g. a device output of 'error count: 0' exits the script with status Error, while an intended failure message of 'failed to apply config' typed without the exact keyword prefix exits Success. In a scheduled-jobs / multi-host fleet context this directly mislabels run results (job history, notifications).
recommendation: In ExitCommand.ExecuteAsync, parse the status keyword from the RAW step.Exit text first, and only substitute variables into the remaining message portion. Decide the bare-message default explicitly: either keep Success but emit a parser/editor warning for `exit: <message>` without a status keyword, or treat keyword-less exit as Failure (safer for the 'abort with reason' mental model). Also support the mapping form's explicit `status:` as authoritative so substitution can never affect it.
user_benefit: Scheduled jobs and fleet runs stop reporting success on failure paths (and vice versa) — exit status becomes deterministic from the script text instead of depending on what a runtime variable happens to start with.

title: on_error: continue is silently ignored by assert and extract failures (script stops anyway)
existing_state: The executor applies on_error only to thrown exceptions (ScriptExecutor.cs:517-531); a command that returns a plain Fail stops the host's script unconditionally (ScriptExecutor.cs:425-431). AssertCommand returns plain CommandResult.Fail for both evaluation errors and failed assertions (Services/Scripting/Commands/AssertCommand.cs:30, 56), and ExtractCommand returns plain Fail for empty-source, no-match-with-required, and regex parse/timeout errors (ExtractCommand.cs:35-37, 65-67, 108-119) — neither ever calls CommandResult.ApplyOnError. Yet the YAML surface actively accepts `on_error` on these steps: it is a generic step-level key (ScriptParser.cs:983) and the assert mapping explicitly parses a nested on_error and hoists it to the step root (ScriptParser.cs:3512-3515). So a user who writes `assert: {...}` / `extract: {...}` with `on_error: continue` gets no warning and the script still aborts mid-run on failure. Related inconsistency: user-cancel in choose and input also bypasses on_error with a plain Fail (ChooseCommand.cs:58-62, InputCommand.cs:61-65) while every other failure in those same commands honors ApplyOnError (ChooseCommand.cs:78, InputCommand.cs:82).
recommendation: Route assert and extract failure returns through CommandResult.ApplyOnError(step, msg) like the other commands (one-line changes at AssertCommand.cs:30/56 and the Fail sites in ExtractCommand). For choose/input cancellation, either honor on_error too or make 'cancel always aborts' an explicit documented rule and have the parser warn when on_error is declared on steps where it cannot apply.
user_benefit: A declared error-handling policy actually works: long fleet scripts with `on_error: continue` on validation/parsing steps no longer die mid-run on the first soft failure, and the behavior matches what the parser/editor accepts.

title: FortiGate parse 'sections' filter leaks excluded config into the result instead of skipping it
existing_state: `parse: { format: fortigate, sections: [...] }` is supposed to return only the listed sections. When a top-level `config` line fails the filter, the parser calls SkipConfigBlock (Services/Scripting/Parsers/FortiGateParser.cs:59-63) — but SkipConfigBlock is an empty placeholder (:248-252, the comment admits it does nothing). Only the `config` header line is skipped; every `set`/`edit`/`unset` line inside the excluded block then executes against the CURRENT context, which is the root result dict (:134-140, :103-132). So filtering `sections: ["system interface"]` on a full FortiGate config returns the wanted section PLUS a root-level soup of keys and edit-entries from every excluded section — and nested `config` lines inside the excluded block are themselves re-evaluated against the filter as if top-level (contextStack is 0), so fragments of excluded sections can appear under wrong names. Additionally, ShouldIncludeSection (:238-242) does bidirectional character-prefix matching (`filters.Any(f => path.StartsWith(f) || f.StartsWith(path))`), so a filter of "sys" matches "system interface", "system admin", etc. — no word-boundary check. Any script that branches on the parsed dictionary gets wrong data.
recommendation: Replace the no-op SkipConfigBlock with real skipping: when a top-level section is filtered out, set a skipDepth counter and consume lines, incrementing on `config` and decrementing on `end`, until depth returns to zero — resuming normal parsing afterwards. Delete the dead ref-parameter signature. Fix ShouldIncludeSection to match on whole space-delimited tokens (e.g. filter must equal the path or be a token-boundary prefix: "system" matches "system interface" but "sys" does not).
user_benefit: The sections filter actually does what it says — scripts that parse device configs get clean, correctly-scoped data instead of polluted root keys that silently corrupt downstream logic (foreach over interfaces, drift comparisons, etc.).

title: Script update-column silently drops grid writes for hosts using the port column (and updates only the first duplicate row)
existing_state: The YAML `update-column` command (Services/Scripting/Commands/UpdateColumnCommand.cs:29) raises ColumnUpdateRequested, which lands in Form1.UpdateHostColumn (Form1.cs:14190-14214). That method finds the target row by re-parsing the grid's Host_IP cell (`HostConnection.Parse(hostIp)` at 14201) and requiring `rowHost.IpAddress == host.IpAddress && rowHost.Port == host.Port` (14202). But at run time the executing host's Port is set from the separate `port` grid column (Form1.cs:13318-13325) or from SSH config (HostConnection.ApplySshConfig, Models/HostConnection.cs:75-77), while `HostConnection.Parse` of a bare IP cell defaults Port to 22 (Models/HostConnection.cs:9,48-51). So any host whose non-22 port comes from the `port` column never matches: the script's grid write-back is a silent no-op — no warning, no log. Additionally, the loop `break`s after the first match (14212), so duplicate Host_IP rows only ever get the first row updated.
recommendation: In UpdateHostColumn, resolve the row's effective port the same way GetHostConnections does (explicit `ip:port` in the cell, else the `port` column value, else 22) before comparing — or better, stop matching by string at all: thread the originating DataGridViewRow (or a row index) through SshColumnUpdateEventArgs since GetHostConnections already iterates concrete rows. Also decide intentionally whether duplicates should all update (remove the `break`) and append an output warning when no row matches so failures are visible.
user_benefit: Scripts that harvest data back into the host grid (inventory, version capture, status columns) currently lose their results without any error for every host on a non-standard SSH port — a silent data-loss path in a core scripting feature.

title: Host grid paste mangles rows: LF-only clipboards collapse into one cell and dropped blank lines shift credentials onto the wrong hosts
existing_state: Both paste implementations corrupt row alignment. HostGridUtilities.PasteClipboardText splits clipboard text with StringSplitOptions.RemoveEmptyEntries (Utilities/HostGridUtilities.cs:234-236): copying a single column from Excel that contains blank cells produces empty lines in the TSV; those are silently removed, so every value after a gap pastes one row higher than it belongs. In the job editor's hosts grid (the consumer, JobEditorDialog.cs:1834) this means pasting a username/password/vault_path column next to existing Host_IP rows silently assigns credentials to the wrong hosts — a scheduled job then runs against hosts with mismatched credentials with no warning. Form1's main hosts grid has its own paste with the identical flaw plus one more: it splits ONLY on "\r\n" with RemoveEmptyEntries (Form1.cs:9612), so clipboard text with bare-LF line endings (VS Code, browsers, Linux terminals, WSL, many password managers) contains no \r\n at all and an entire multi-line host list is dumped into a single cell with embedded newlines. The grid is the credential source for executions (GetHostConnections reads these cells, Form1.cs:13313-13359) and SaveCurrentCsv persists the corrupted layout. Secondary defects: BuildClipboardText's all-selected branch also skips empty rows on copy (HostGridUtilities.cs:186-189), so even an in-app copy/paste round-trip shifts rows; and PasteClipboardText sets grid.AllowUserToAddRows = false at :238 and restores it at :265 with no try/finally, so an exception mid-paste permanently removes the new-row affordance.
recommendation: In both paste implementations, split on any line-ending convention (`text.Split(new[] { "\r\n", "\n", "\r" }, StringSplitOptions.None)`), preserve interior empty lines as empty cells so row alignment is kept, and only trim a single trailing empty entry (clipboard TSV conventionally ends with a newline). Wrap the AllowUserToAddRows toggle in try/finally in HostGridUtilities.PasteClipboardText, and remove (or restrict to trailing) the isEmpty skip in BuildClipboardText's all-selected branch so copy/paste round-trips are position-faithful.
user_benefit: Prevents the worst kind of fleet-tool error: SSH credentials and per-host variables silently landing on the wrong host rows after an ordinary spreadsheet paste — and makes pasting from any non-Windows source work at all.

title: A dozen UI handlers reload config.json from disk mid-session; a single transient read failure makes them overwrite the entire config with defaults
existing_state: Preset/folder drag-reorder (Form1.cs:4946, 4954, 4973, 5010), rename ordering (Form1.cs:5085), favorites refresh/reorder (Form1.cs:5197, 5477), folder summary (Form1.cs:11159), and every folder execution (Form1.cs:12836, 12866) call `_configService.Load()` — a full disk re-read — instead of `GetCurrent()`. `ConfigurationService.Load()` catches ALL exceptions (corrupt JSON, or a transient sharing violation from sync/backup/AV tooling holding config.json), backs the file up to config.json.corrupt, and silently returns a DEFAULT configuration while replacing the in-memory cache (Services/ConfigurationService.cs:91-102). The resulting `ConfigLoadError` is only ever surfaced at startup (Form1.cs:350-354). So during something as mundane as dragging a preset, a momentary read failure yields a default config that the handler immediately mutates and saves (e.g., ReorderFolders at Form1.cs:4946-4948) — writing defaults over config.json: all presets, all environments including host inventories, Vault and notification settings. The next save then copies the defaulted file over config.json.bak (Services/ConfigurationService.cs:116-120), destroying the last good backup. Even absent a failure, each Load() discards any in-memory config mutations not yet saved and re-inflates the compressed saved-state blob from disk on every drag step — pure churn.
recommendation: Replace every mid-session `_configService.Load()` with `GetCurrent()` (or the existing `Update(...)` helper, which is the intended pattern). In ConfigurationService.Load(), when a cached config already exists, treat a read/parse failure as an error (rethrow or surface ConfigLoadError immediately) rather than silently substituting defaults that callers will persist. (The atomic-write/backup-restore half of this hole is covered by BUG-001.)
user_benefit: Eliminates a one-shot total-config-wipe path (presets, environments, host lists, Vault settings) that can be triggered by OneDrive/antivirus briefly locking config.json while you drag a preset, and removes repeated full-config disk reloads during normal UI interactions.

title: Scheduled jobs do not block interactive presets — an unattended run pops a terminal window and hangs the job queue
existing_state: The single-host-only preflight for `interactive:` only fires when `hostList.Count != 1` (Services/SshExecutionService.cs:564), and the unattended preflight covers LocalCmd confirmation only (SshExecutionService.cs:937-955). `JobExecutionService` runs presets via `sshService.ExecutePresetAsync(..., allowFileSelectionDialogs: false)` (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:687) which routes scripts to `ExecuteScriptAsync` (SshExecutionService.cs:476-478) — so a scheduled job targeting one host with an `interactive:` preset sails past every guard (grep confirms JobExecutionService contains zero interactive checks). At runtime the step marshals onto the main form's UI thread (InteractiveTerminalService.cs:3615-3638) and shows a real terminal window (1775-1907); window mode then awaits `formClosedTcs` with no timeout (1946). An overnight/unattended scheduled run therefore pops a terminal on the desktop and blocks forever until a human closes it — while holding the scheduler's `_concurrencyGate` semaphore (JobExecutionService.cs:84, 342-355), so subsequent scheduled jobs queue behind it indefinitely. Inconsistently, folder-type jobs ARE protected because `ExecuteFolderAsync` blocks interactive presets regardless of host count (SshExecutionService.cs:662-682).
recommendation: Add an unattended-run preflight for interactive (and browser-callback) steps, exactly like the existing LocalCmd one: pass an `unattended`/`allowInteractive: false` flag from JobExecutionService through `ExecutePresetAsync`/`ExecuteScriptAsync`, and fail the job up front with a clear message ('interactive steps are not supported in scheduled jobs'). Optionally also warn at job-save time in JobEditorDialog using `ScriptDependencyAnalyzer.UsesInteractive`.
user_benefit: A single mis-assigned preset currently wedges the entire scheduler overnight (jobs queue behind a window nobody is there to close). With the guard, the job fails fast with an actionable message instead of silently stalling automation.

title: Pool lease race: parallel presets on one host release the wrong lease and leak standalone SSH connections
existing_state: `SshConnectionPool.CreateSessionAsync` leases a key with `_leasedKeys.TryAdd(key, true)`; if the key is already leased it builds a standalone client via `CreateConnectionAsync` (`SshConnectionPool.cs:244-252`) that is never put into `_connections`. Every caller's `finally` then unconditionally calls `ReleaseSession(host, username, password)` (`SshExecutionService.cs:1570`, `:2154`), which does `_leasedKeys.TryRemove(key, ...)` (`SshConnectionPool.cs:275`) — removing the *single* lease entry regardless of which caller owns it. This is reachable today: the folder-run "Run presets in parallel" option (`ExecuteFolderAsync`, runPresetsInParallel at `:713`) runs multiple presets against the *same* host concurrently, each calling `ExecutePresetOnHostAsync`->`ExecuteWithPool`/`ExecuteScriptWithPool`->`CreateSessionAsync` with an identical key. Sequence: preset A leases and uses the pooled connection; B and C get standalone connections; B finishes first and `ReleaseSession` clears A's lease; a later preset D then re-leases and reuses the pooled connection that A is *still actively driving* — two callers issuing commands on the same Rebex scripting stream -> interleaved/garbled output and wrong per-preset results. Separately, the standalone clients (B, C) are leaked: `SshShellSession.Dispose` (`:1446-1474`) disposes only the scripting/terminal owners, never the `Ssh` client, and these standalone clients are not in the pool to be swept, so each collision leaks a live SSH connection until process exit.
recommendation: Track lease ownership per session instance, not per key: return a lease token/handle from `CreateSessionAsync` and have `ReleaseSession` only clear the lease it actually created (e.g. only the caller that won `TryAdd`). For the standalone-collision path, either dispose the standalone `Ssh` client explicitly when its session ends (have the session own and disconnect it), or serialize same-key sessions so a second concurrent caller waits rather than spawning an untracked connection. Add a regression test that runs two concurrent `CreateSessionAsync` calls for the same key and asserts the pooled connection is never handed to two live sessions and that standalone clients are disconnected.
user_benefit: Stops corrupted/mixed-up output when running multiple presets in parallel against one host, and stops the app from leaking live SSH sessions to that host on every collision.

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: ReleaseSession (SshConnectionPool.cs:272-280) unconditionally removes the single per-key lease, and both callers' finally blocks (SshExecutionService.cs:1570, 2154) release even when they were standalone (non-lease-owning) callers, so a finishing preset clears the active holder's lease and a later same-key CreateSessionAsync re-leases the pooled Ssh client the holder is still driving; standalone clients from the collision path (SshConnectionPool.cs:251) are never tracked, never disposed by SshShellSession.Dispose (1446-1474) or by callers, and the cleanup sweep only iterates _connections, so each collision leaks a live SSH connection. Two nuances: the garbled-output symptom assumes Rebex tolerates a second VirtualTerminal.Bind on one Ssh (it may instead throw, spuriously failing the later preset — still wrong results), and the reuse-while-active sequence needs staggered preset-task starts, whereas the leak fires on essentially every parallel-preset collision. High severity is justified either way.

title: Pool health check sends `echo 1` and uses a prompt regex missing arrow terminators — permanent connection churn for some devices
existing_state: `IsConnectionHealthyAsync` actively probes a pooled connection at most every 30s by `scripting.Send("echo 1\r")` and waiting for `ScriptEvent.FromRegex(@"[#$>%]\s*$")` with a 5s timeout (`SshConnectionPool.cs:552-558`). That terminator set omits the arrow-style prompt terminators the rest of the engine explicitly supports — `PromptDetector.PromptTerminators` includes arrow glyphs (`Utilities/PromptDetector.cs:11`) and `SshShellSession.Patterns.ShellPrompt` matches them (`SshShellSession.cs:123`). So a host with a starship/oh-my-zsh arrow prompt never matches the health-check regex; `ReadUntil` times out at 5s, the catch returns false, and the connection is removed and recreated (`GetOrCreateAsync :156-160`). Every reuse after the 30s window therefore tears down and re-handshakes the connection, defeating pooling entirely for those hosts. Additionally `echo 1` is a literal command injected into every pooled host's session — on network appliances (FortiGate/Cisco) `echo` is often invalid and may be logged as a failed command on the device.
recommendation: Use the same prompt-terminator class the engine already standardized on (include the arrow glyphs, ideally reuse `PromptDetector`/`Patterns.ShellPromptPattern`) for the health probe, and prefer a no-op that doesn't pollute device logs — send a bare CR (or the session's keepalive) and wait for the known prompt regex rather than `echo 1`. Better, reuse the connection's already-detected `_promptPattern` instead of a hardcoded regex.
user_benefit: Pooling actually works for hosts with modern arrow prompts instead of silently re-connecting on every command batch, and stops injecting bogus `echo` commands into appliance logs.

title: Host CSV save truncates the file in place — a failed save destroys the host inventory with no backup
existing_state: CsvManager.SaveToFile opens the target with `new StreamWriter(filePath, false, ...)` (Services/CsvManager.cs:78), which truncates the existing file immediately, then streams the grid out row by row (:83-102). There is no temp-file swap and no backup copy anywhere in the path (Form1.SaveCsvToFile at Form1.cs:9310-9325 calls it directly). If the process dies or the disk fills mid-write, the operator's source-of-truth host list is gone; the catch in TrySaveCsvToPath (Form1.cs:9303-9306) shows "Failed to save file" after the original content has already been destroyed. This is the file driving which hosts every command and scheduled job targets.
recommendation: Write to filePath + ".tmp" and finish with File.Replace (mirroring JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic, Utilities/JsonFileWriter.cs:21-88 — extract a text variant or generalize it), optionally keeping a .bak of the previous CSV. One method change in CsvManager.SaveToFile plus a unit test for the interrupted-write case.
user_benefit: A crash or full disk during Save can no longer delete the entire host inventory; the worst case becomes "old file still intact".

title: Installing an update exits via Environment.Exit, skipping the shutdown save — session state lost and stale shutdown anchor fabricates 'missed run' history
existing_state: UpdateService.LaunchUpdaterAndExit starts the PowerShell updater and calls Environment.Exit(0) (Services/UpdateService.cs:423-424), invoked from UpdateDialog after install confirmation (UpdateDialog.cs:576). Environment.Exit does not raise FormClosing, so Form1_FormClosing (Form1.cs:3932-3948) never runs: SaveConfiguration is skipped — losing window geometry/splitters, the active environment's grid snapshot, SavedState (host grid/selection/preset), recent files, sort order, username, and the host-password-to-Credential-Manager migration (Form1.cs:14625-14702) — _jobExecutionService.Stop() is never called, and LastAppShutdownUtc is never written (Form1.cs:3946). On the next launch, RecordMissedSchedulerRunsOnStartup (Form1.cs:15258-15283) anchors missed-run detection to the PREVIOUS clean shutdown, and DetectMissedRunSummaries counts every cron occurrence since that anchor with no check that the job actually ran (Services/SchedulingService.cs:148-181) — so every recurring run that genuinely executed during the pre-update session gets a false 'skipped N runs' summary written into job history. The pre-install ConfirmExitWorkflow hook (UpdateDialog.cs:563 -> Form1.cs:14891-14917) only resolves dirty CSV/preset prompts; it does not save config.
recommendation: Before calling LaunchUpdaterAndExit in UpdateDialog (or inside the _confirmExitBeforeInstall callback in Form1), run the same shutdown sequence as Form1_FormClosing: stop the job execution service, set LastAppShutdownUtc, and call SaveConfiguration — then exit. Alternatively have LaunchUpdaterAndExit accept a pre-exit callback, or set _exitConfirmed and call the main form's Close() so the normal FormClosing path runs, starting the updater from FormClosed.
user_benefit: Updating the app stops silently discarding the session's layout/host-grid state and stops polluting job history with bogus 'skipped run' records for jobs that actually ran.

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: LaunchUpdaterAndExit calls Environment.Exit(0) (UpdateService.cs:423-424), which bypasses Form1_FormClosing — the sole writer of LastAppShutdownUtc and the shutdown SaveConfiguration (Form1.cs:3946-3947) — and ConfirmExitWorkflow (Form1.cs:14891-14917) saves nothing. title: Renaming an environment silently breaks script environment pins and folder overrides — presets then run against whatever environment is active
existing_state: EnvironmentService.RenameEnvironment (Services/EnvironmentService.cs:216-255) re-keys the map and follows the active/base pointers, but nothing cascades to the two other places environment names are stored: YAML scripts' `environment:` headers (preset content) and per-folder FolderInfo.BaseEnvironment overrides (Models/FolderInfo.cs:12). After a rename, loading a preset that declares the old name hits the missing-environment branch in ApplyPresetEnvironmentOnPresetLoad (Form1.cs:2186-2192): a status-bar message is shown, the auto-switch is skipped, and the preset remains loaded against the CURRENTLY ACTIVE environment's host grid. In a multi-host fleet tool this means a script pinned to e.g. "staging" can be executed against the production host list with only a transient status-bar hint, and folder base-environment overrides dangle silently.
recommendation: On rename, cascade: update FolderInfo.BaseEnvironment entries matching the old name (Services/PresetManager folders via the same config Update), and scan preset Commands for a YAML `environment:` header equal to the old name, offering a one-click rewrite (the parser already exposes TryGetScriptDeclaredEnvironment, Form1.cs:2201+). Independently, harden the failure mode: when a preset's declared environment is missing, raise a modal/blocking confirmation before run rather than a status-bar note.
user_benefit: Eliminates a wrong-target hazard: renaming an environment can currently cause environment-pinned scripts to run against the wrong host fleet with effectively no warning.

missing environment -> status-bar message only; preset stays loaded on active environment

title: Interactive window errors vanish into a deliberate no-op and the step still reports success
existing_state: When the terminal pump crashes or the connection drops in window mode (shared or separate, no `command:`), the error is invisible and the script step succeeds anyway. The chain: every `[interactive-error] {ex.Message}` is routed through `AppendOutputSafe` (Services/Terminal/InteractiveTerminalService.cs:1940, 2123, 2246, 1037) into `InteractiveTerminalForm.AppendOutput`, which is an intentional no-op (Forms/InteractiveTerminalForm.cs:168-172) — the window just closes with no explanation. The close reason is set to error/disconnected (InteractiveTerminalService.cs:1935-1943, 1687-1704, 1990-1993), but `RunSeparateAsync` returns `InteractiveTerminalRunResult.Ok(transcript, closeReason)` regardless of that reason (InteractiveTerminalService.cs:416), as does `RunSharedAsync` (line 310). `InteractiveCommand` then maps `Success == true` to `CommandResult.Ok()` (Services/Scripting/Commands/InteractiveCommand.cs:29-48), so the script continues as if the session completed normally. Capture mode does check error/disconnected (InteractiveTerminalService.cs:553-561) — window mode is the gap. The only trace is the `close_reason` field buried in the history's Interactive tab. The headless pump even discards the exception object entirely (`catch (Exception)` without binding, InteractiveTerminalService.cs:2090-2093).
recommendation: Two small changes: (1) in `RunSeparateAsync`/`RunSharedAsync`, treat close reason `error` as a step failure (and at minimum emit a `ScriptOutputType.Error` line for `disconnected` so it appears in the run output), mirroring the capture-mode checks at 553-561; (2) surface the error text — either implement `AppendOutput` as a one-line status overlay/message box before close, or route the `[interactive-error]` string into `context.EmitOutput(..., Error)` since the form path is dead. Thread the actual exception message into the failure result instead of the generic strings.
user_benefit: Today a mid-session SSH failure makes the terminal window silently disappear and the rest of the script keeps running against a fiction of success — later steps then fail confusingly or, worse, the run is recorded green. Users get the real error at the moment it happens and a correctly failed step.
mockup_idea: Before: terminal window simply gone, run output shows nothing. After: run output shows 'interactive step failed: <Rebex message> (connection lost)' in red and the step is marked failed.

evidence.note: AppendOutput is a documented no-op — the only sink for interactive error text
pump exception: close reason Error, message sent to the no-op, window closed
RunSharedAsync/RunSeparateAsync return Ok() regardless of error/disconnected close reason
Success==true maps straight to CommandResult.Ok()
capture mode correctly fails on disconnected/error — window mode lacks the same check; headless pump discards the exception detail

verification.notes: Fully traced: every [interactive-error] message dead-ends in the documented no-op AppendOutput (InteractiveTerminalForm.cs:168-172 via AppendOutputSafe at InteractiveTerminalService.cs:3281), and RunSharedAsync/RunSeparateAsync (lines 310/416) return Ok() — Success hardcoded true — regardless of the error/disconnected close reason, so InteractiveCommand.cs:29-48 reports the step green; capture mode's checks at 553-561 confirm window mode is the gap and the recommendation is not implemented. One nuance: success-on-'disconnected' is partly intentional since a normal user exit (Ctrl+D/exit) also yields that close reason — the unambiguous wrong-success case is the 'error' reason, which the recommendation already handles by failing only on 'error' and merely surfacing 'disconnected'.

title: Password-only Vault secrets can never authenticate (all-or-nothing username+password read)
existing_state: VaultCredentialProvider always requests BOTH keys: `var keys = new[] { usernameKey, passwordKey }` with defaults username/password (Services/Vault/VaultCredentialProvider.cs:47, 86-87). VaultService.ReadSecretKeysAsync is all-or-nothing: if ANY requested key is absent from the secret it throws a VaultException 'Secret ... has no key ...' (Services/Vault/VaultService.cs:132-139). That exception is then swallowed by the provider's catch (line 59-63) -> returns false -> silent fallback to the toolbar default password. Net effect: a very common Vault layout where the secret stores only `password` (and the username comes from the grid's username column) is impossible to use via vault_path — the read always throws on the missing `username` key, and the user gets no message explaining why. The `result.TryGetValue(usernameKey,...)` tolerance at lines 51-52 is unreachable because the read already threw.
recommendation: Make the username key optional. Either (a) read keys independently so a missing username key yields a null username instead of failing the whole read, or (b) when usernameKey wasn't explicitly specified via the `#user,pass` suffix, request only the password key and let host.Username keep the grid value. Add a ReadSecretKeysAsync overload (or a `requiredKeys` set) so the provider can tolerate a missing username while still requiring the password.
user_benefit: Lets operators store just a password in Vault (the most common pattern) with the username coming from the host grid, instead of being forced to duplicate usernames into every secret or silently failing.

evidence.note: always asks for username+password; success requires non-empty password
throws if any requested key missing -> whole read fails

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds exactly: VaultCredentialProvider.cs:47 always requests both keys (defaults at 86-87), VaultService.ReadSecretKeysAsync throws on any absent key (VaultService.cs:132-139, and the cache can never satisfy a key the secret lacks), the catch at VaultCredentialProvider.cs:59-63 reduces it to Debug.WriteLine + false, and both consumers fall through silently — Form1.GetHostConnections (Form1.cs:13332-13357) drops to the credential-manager/grid password and ultimately the toolbar default (tsbPassword.Text at Form1.cs:12404), and JobExecutionService has the same exposure at lines 512-522 and 628-639 (CredentialMode.Vault). No overload, requiredKeys option, or workaround exists (the #user,pass suffix still requires both keys), and the test suite has no password-only-secret coverage. High is justified: a standard password-only secret layout silently fails and the app then authenticates with a different password than the operator intended.

title: JsonFileWriter's fallback path can destroy both the old and the new file when File.Replace fails
existing_state: When File.Replace throws (classic Windows trigger: antivirus/indexer briefly locks the just-written .tmp or the target), WriteJsonAtomic falls back to File.Delete(path) at Utilities/JsonFileWriter.cs:69 followed by File.Move(tempPath, path) at :72. Two failure modes: (1) a crash between Delete and Move leaves no file at all; (2) if Delete succeeds but Move throws (the same transient lock on the .tmp that made Replace fail), the finally block at :74-87 deletes the temp file — the original is already gone and the new content is actively destroyed. For history run payloads written with createBackup: false (Services/HistoryStorageService.cs:468, Services/JobHistoryService.cs:227) there is no .bak to recover from. The bare catch blocks at :43 and :63 also discard the reason Replace failed, so the destructive fallback engages on any exception including UnauthorizedAccessException.
recommendation: Restructure the fallback so the live file is never deleted: move the original to {path}.bak (atomic rename on same volume) instead of File.Delete, then move the temp into place; on failure, move the .bak back and rethrow or report. In the finally block, only delete the temp file if the swap succeeded — when it failed, leave the .tmp on disk as the surviving copy of the data. Narrow the catch around File.Replace to IOException/UnauthorizedAccessException and log the exception so repeat failures are diagnosable.
user_benefit: Eliminates a silent data-destruction path in the primitive that guards execution history and job history — an AV scan racing a save should never be able to delete a history file outright.

evidence.note: Replace-fail fallback: Delete(path) :69, Move(temp) :72, finally deletes temp :74-87 even when Move failed; bare catch :43,:63
Per-run history payloads written with createBackup: false — total loss if the fallback misfires
Job history payloads also createBackup: false

verification.notes: Traced and confirmed: bare catches at JsonFileWriter.cs:43/:63 route any Replace failure into Delete(path) at :69 + Move at :72, and the finally at :74-87 deletes the .tmp even when the Move failed. The deterministic both-copies-lost case is an AV/indexer holding the target with FILE_SHARE_DELETE (Delete succeeds as delete-pending, Move throws "destination exists", finally deletes the unlocked .tmp, original vanishes when the scanner's handle closes). One nuance: in the sub-case where the .tmp itself is still locked, the finally delete also fails and the .tmp survives orphaned — but nothing in the codebase ever reads .tmp files, so it is still app-level loss of the live file. All cited createBackup:false call sites verified (HistoryStorageService.cs:468, JobHistoryService.cs:227/:280); the recommendation is not implemented.

title: Flow Canvas "Test this step" on a nested block executes ALL later blocks inside its container — the scope-disable logic is vacuous (and once fixed, the disables would leak into later full runs)
existing_state: ExecuteCanvasTestStep truncates the script only at TOP-LEVEL granularity (Form1.cs:7072, 7084; TryBuildYamlThroughTopLevelStep at 7356-7394 keeps the entire top-level step containing the target). Out-of-scope nested blocks are supposed to be disabled via BuildTestStepAllowedRoots + IsStepPathAllowed (Form1.cs:7131-7142). But BuildTestStepAllowedRoots adds the target's whole top-level step path as a root (`roots.Add(currentStepPath)` with currentStepPath = "steps/{topLevelStepIndex}", Form1.cs:7409-7410), and IsStepPathAllowed treats every root as a PREFIX (`stepPath.StartsWith(root + "/")`, Form1.cs:7451). Therefore every descendant of that step — sibling branches AND all siblings AFTER the selected block — is 'allowed', `testScopeDisabledNodes` is always empty, and the careful per-branch root computation at 7415-7438 is dead code (verified by tracing the code: for target steps/2/then/1 the roots set contains steps/2, which prefix-matches everything beneath it). Net effect: testing a block nested in a foreach/do or if/then runs the entire container against the live SSH host, including destructive steps placed after the one being tested. A second latent defect sits in the same method: the test-scope disables are merged into the persistent `_pendingDisabledBlocks` staging set (Form1.cs:7133-7142) and the `existingDisabledNodes` snapshot taken at 7137 is never used to restore it — the finally only resets the prompt anchor (7156-7159), and post-run cleanup deliberately leaves `_pendingDisabledBlocks` alone (Form1.cs:13826-13837) while the next full run re-applies every staged id (Form1.cs:12322-12361). Today this leak is masked only because the disable set is always empty; the moment the scoping bug is fixed, sibling branches disabled for a test would stay silently disabled for subsequent full runs.
recommendation: Make intermediate container paths exact-match-only: in IsStepPathAllowed, only the FINAL target path (and fully-allowed prerequisite top-level steps steps/0..N-1) should be prefix roots; the chain of enclosing containers (steps/N, steps/N/do/2, ...) must match exactly so untargeted descendants stay disallowed. Keep the existing `{listScope}/0..targetIndexInScope` roots for earlier siblings. In the same change, restore `_pendingDisabledBlocks` to the pre-merge snapshot in the finally block (the snapshot already exists at Form1.cs:7137) — or pass the test-scope disables to ExecutePresetOnRowsAsync as an explicit parameter unioned only for that one run — so the now-real disables cannot leak into later full runs. Add a unit test asserting testScopeDisabledNodes is non-empty for a nested target with a later sibling, and that _pendingDisabledBlocks is unchanged after the test completes.
user_benefit: "Test this step" is the safety feature users rely on to poke one command at a real device; today it can fire every subsequent command in the loop/branch (e.g. a config-write right after the show command you wanted to test). Fixing it without the restore would instead silently skip sibling branches in later full runs — this closes both holes together.
