title: Deleting one wire silently drops every downstream block from the exported YAML — only the first orphan gets a warning
existing_state: Export order is built by walking edges from the Start block (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1126-1137, BuildChain at 1696-1705); any node not reached is excluded from the YAML. The 'unreachable node' warning at FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1140-1152 only fires when the node ALSO has zero incoming edges (`!visited.Contains(nid) && !incomingCount.ContainsKey(nid)` at line 1145). So if a user deletes the wire between step 3 and step 4 of a 10-step preset and hits Run/Apply, only the orphan-chain head (step 4) gets a warning; steps 5-10 have incoming edges (from other orphans) and are dropped with NO diagnostic at all. The diagnostic is Warning-level, so export still succeeds (Success = no errors, FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1382-1385) and Form1.ApplyFlowCanvasGraph overwrites the editor text with the truncated YAML (Form1.cs:6932, 6966-6969). The preset layout saved at Form1.cs:6989-7001 stores only positions/comments — block content lives in the YAML snippets — so once the canvas reloads from the truncated YAML, the dropped steps are unrecoverable.
recommendation: In ExportGraphToYaml, warn for EVERY excluded executable node, not just edge-less ones: compute the orphan set as all non-hidden, non-child, non-comment nodes absent from `visited` and emit one diagnostic each (or one grouped diagnostic listing them). Drop the `!incomingCount.ContainsKey(nid)` clause at FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1145. Consider escalating to Error severity (blocking apply) when the orphan set contains snippet-bearing top-level steps, or have Form1 require an explicit confirmation before overwriting txtCommand when any node was excluded.
user_benefit: Prevents silent loss of script steps from a single accidental edge deletion — today most of a preset can vanish from the YAML with one easy-to-miss warning about a single node.
mockup_idea: Before/after of the apply flow: 'before' shows the current single toast warning naming one node id while 9 blocks quietly disappear from the YAML preview; 'after' shows a blocking confirmation dialog listing all excluded blocks by label with Keep-in-YAML / Remove choices.

evidence.note: chain built from Start only; warning gated on having zero incoming edges, so downstream orphans are silently excluded
BuildChain DFS — defines `visited`
graphChanged=true (an edge delete is a change) overwrites txtCommand with the truncated YAML; warnings do not block

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds exactly as written. Export emits only nodes reached by the Start-rooted DFS (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1253 loop over orderedIds), and the unreachable-node warning at line 1145 is gated on having zero incoming edges, so in a broken chain only the head orphan is named — every downstream block is dropped with no diagnostic. Warnings never block (Success = no Errors, line 50), Form1 overwrites txtCommand on graphChanged (6966-6969) for both Apply and Run paths, ExtractLayout saves no snippets, and the React side has no reachability guard (success warnings go to a per-node badge + console.warn). Minor mitigation: the orphaned blocks stay on the canvas until it reloads, so loss is only permanent after close/reopen — which the finding already states. High severity is appropriate.

title: Disabled-block state is persisted and restored by unstable raw node id — the wrong block gets silently skipped after the preset's YAML changes
existing_state: Layout autosave persists node positions keyed by the stable `stepPath:blockType` tuple, but `disabledBlocks` and `expandedNodes` are flat arrays of raw live node ids (FlowCanvas/src/utils/layoutAutosave.ts:51-61). On the next open, the host re-applies them by raw id: `MergeAuxiliaryLayout` stamps `data.disabled = true` on whichever node currently has that id (Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:5444-5456), and React then rebuilds its disabled set from that stamp (stores/messageBridge.ts:169-177). Node ids are reassigned sequentially on every import (`node-{_idCounter++}`, FlowCanvasBridge.cs:331), so any change that shifts step order between the autosave and the next open — editing the preset in the text editor, deleting a step, inserting one above — moves the disabled flag onto a DIFFERENT block, which the executor then skips during runs. The codebase already knows ids are unstable: position merge was migrated to the tuple key for exactly this reason (`TryMergeLayoutByTuple`, FlowCanvasBridge.cs:5403-5441, with 'pre-migration entry: no stable key' comment at :5409), but disabled/expanded were left id-keyed. Compounding it, deleting a node never purges its id from `disabledBlocks`/`breakpoints`/`expandedNodes` (graphSlice.ts:447-456 filters only selectedNodeIds), so a deleted disabled block's stale id is persisted by every autosave (layoutAutosave.ts:60) and lands on whichever block inherits that id after the ids shift.
recommendation: Key disabled (and expanded) persistence by the same `stepPath:blockType` tuple as positions: include the tuple in the autosave payload (layoutAutosave.ts) and match on it in MergeAuxiliaryLayout instead of raw id, with the same 'vanished tuple -> drop' safety rule TryMergeLayoutByTuple uses. Separately, purge removed node ids from `disabledBlocks`, `breakpoints`, and `expandedNodes` inside `removeNodes`/`onNodesChange` remove handling in graphSlice.ts.
user_benefit: A block the user never disabled can currently be skipped in a multi-host run — silently producing an incomplete deployment/audit — just because they edited the script after disabling a different block.

verification.notes: Root cause is real and all cited code checks out (raw-id persistence of disabledBlocks/expandedNodes, id-stamped restore in MergeAuxiliaryLayout, per-import id reassignment, no purge of deleted ids in graphSlice), but three details are wrong: (1) the restore only runs for Manual-layout-mode presets with saved positions (Form1.cs:6856-6884) — in Auto-flow (the default) disabled state is silently dropped on reopen, never mis-applied; (2) deletes and type-changing inserts fail the tuple-safety check (TryMergeLayoutByTuple Safe=false) so the layout is dropped rather than mis-stamped — the wrong-block stamp needs a same-type reorder/insert or the stale-id-after-canvas-delete+Apply path, which does hold; (3) across an app restart the restored disabled stamp never reaches the executor at all (restoreDisabledBlocks in debugSlice.ts:134-139 sends nothing to C#, and runs are fed only from the live-toggle _pendingDisabledBlocks set, Form1.cs:6779/12352-12361) — so the cross-restart symptom is a greyed block that actually RUNS, while the genuine wrong-block skip happens within a session via the retained raw-id _pendingDisabledBlocks, plus a UI/C# toggle desync where re-enabling a restored block secretly disables it in the executor. Net: the bug cluster is real and severity high is justified (wrong block silently skipped or silently executed), but the causal chain and triggers need the corrections above; the recommendation is unimplemented and sound, and should also cover _pendingDisabledBlocks and the toggle desync. title: Breakpoints leak across preset switches on both sides of the bridge — runs pause at invisible breakpoints and the first gutter click does nothing
existing_state: When a new graph loads, `resetGraphSessionState` clears dirty/history/execution/timeline/exportStatus/iterations (FlowCanvas/src/stores/messageBridge.ts:74-81) and the load handler explicitly re-restores `disabledBlocks` and `expandedNodes` from node data — the comment at messageBridge.ts:164-168 documents that this exact leak was fixed for those two Sets because preset node ids collide. The `breakpoints` Set got no such treatment: debugSlice has no clear or restore action for it (stores/slices/debugSlice.ts:36, 41-56) and nothing in the load path touches it. title: No global exception handler: any unhandled error is a stock crash with no save, no log — and two startup paths throw unhandled
existing_state: There are zero registrations of Application.ThreadException, AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException, or Application.SetUnhandledExceptionMode anywhere in the codebase (grep across all .cs files returns no hits). Program.Main runs Application.Run(new Form1()) bare (Program.cs:59). Concrete unhandled startup throws exist today: (a) ScintillaNativeBootstrap.ExtractEmbeddedNativeLibraries throws InvalidOperationException when both extraction roots are unwritable (Utilities/ScintillaNativeBootstrap.cs:84-86, called from Program.cs:58) — hard crash before any window; (b) AppDataPaths.ValidateStartupStorageWritable returns true without probing in standard builds (Utilities/AppDataPaths.cs:99-100), so a locked-down or full %LocalAppData% surfaces as a raw exception inside the Form1 constructor (GetAppFolder/Directory.CreateDirectory via ConfigurationService at Form1.cs:344, or the first-run default-config Save at ConfigurationService.cs:48-53). At runtime, any stray exception on the UI thread kills a process that may hold an unsaved host grid, running SSH sessions, and the scheduler — with no log, no state flush, and (because LastAppShutdownUtc is only written in FormClosing, Form1.cs:3946) corrupted missed-run bookkeeping on the next start.
recommendation: In Program.Main: wrap the bootstrap (ConfigureSatelliteDirectory onward) in try/catch that shows an actionable error dialog; register Application.ThreadException and AppDomain.CurrentDomain.UnhandledException handlers that write the exception to a crash log under AppDataPaths.GetAppFolder() and attempt a best-effort SaveConfiguration before exiting; extend ValidateStartupStorageWritable to probe %LocalAppData%\SSH_Helper in standard builds too (TryEnsureFolderWritable already exists and is only wired for portable mode).
user_benefit: Crashes stop silently destroying in-session work and become diagnosable; the two real startup-crash paths (unwritable AppData, failed native extraction) get a clear message instead of a stack-trace dialog or instant process death.

title: Preset-to-canvas load failures are swallowed, leaving the previous preset's graph live — Apply then overwrites the new preset's YAML with the old script
existing_state: LoadCurrentScriptIntoCanvas wraps the whole bridge conversion in a bare `catch { /* Silently fail — canvas will show empty state */ }` (Form1.cs:6844-6889). The comment is wrong for the common case: on failure no LoadGraph message is sent at all, so an open canvas keeps rendering whatever was loaded before. TextToGraph calls ScriptParser.Parse directly (Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:381-391), which can throw on YAML that passes the lightweight IsYamlScript heuristic gate (Form1.cs:6838) — e.g. a hand-edited preset with a syntax error. Concrete hazard: switch from preset A to broken preset B with the canvas open (LoadPresetIntoEditor, Form1.cs:2148-2160) — `_activePresetName` is now B but the canvas still shows A's blocks; pressing Apply or Run from the canvas calls ApplyFlowCanvasGraph, which exports the stale graph and writes it into txtCommand when graphChanged is true (Form1.cs:6966-6969) — replacing the newly selected preset's content with the previous preset's script; saving the preset persists the cross-preset overwrite. Relatedly, BuildNodeIdToStepPathMap has a swallow-all catch returning an empty map (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:5224-5227), so a run on un-graphable YAML silently loses all canvas highlighting/output attribution. The same swallow also hides genuine bridge bugs as a mystery 'empty canvas'.
recommendation: In the catch block, capture the exception and send the canvas an explicit failure state instead of nothing: at minimum `LoadGraph(new JArray(), new JArray())` plus an error banner naming the preset and parse error (or a dedicated load-failed message), so the stale graph is cleared and Apply cannot export stale content. Log the exception via SshDebugLog. Consider an `importFailed` flag in load-graph so React can disable Apply/Run until a valid graph loads.
user_benefit: Eliminates a confusing and dangerous state where the canvas displays one preset while edits/runs target another — preventing a silent failure from escalating into real data loss when applying from a stale canvas replaces one preset's YAML with another preset's script.
mockup_idea: Small before/after of the canvas: before — old graph silently shown for the wrong preset; after — empty canvas with a banner 'Could not load "<preset>" into the canvas: YAML parse error at line N' and a Retry link.

title: History lies after a crash: the interrupted run vanishes, and the next startup logs false 'Skipped' entries for runs that actually executed
existing_state: Two crash-path defects compound. (1) Crash recovery in Initialize() finds orphaned RunningState and raises only a transient JobStateChanged(Failed, 'Application crashed during execution') (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:153-168); it never raises JobCompleted, and JobHistoryService persists runs only from JobCompleted (Services/JobHistoryService.cs:36-47). The crashed run therefore leaves zero trace in run history — a cron job that dies mid-run every night shows a clean history, and the Job List 'Last Result' column (JobListDialog.cs:755-763 reads the newest history record) keeps showing the previous night's 'OK (n/n)'. (2) LastAppShutdownUtc is written only in the graceful FormClosing path (Form1.cs:3946). After a crash, the next launch anchors missed-run detection to the PREVIOUS graceful shutdown (Form1.cs:15265-15272), so the detection window swallows the entire crashed session — every recurring run that genuinely executed during that session is re-counted and written into history as 'Skipped (N runs)' (Form1.cs:15276-15282, rendered orange in JobListDialog). Together, after any crash the history both omits the run that died and fabricates misses for runs that succeeded.
recommendation: (1) In Initialize(), synthesize a failed JobRunResult (Success=false, ErrorMessage='Application crashed during execution', StartedUtc from RunningState.StartedUtc, CompletedUtc now, empty HostOutputs — mirror the OnJobFailed shape at JobExecutionService.cs:909-927) and raise JobCompleted so the existing history pipeline records it. (2) Heartbeat the downtime anchor: update LastAppShutdownUtc (or a dedicated LastSchedulerEvaluationUtc) at the end of each 30-second evaluation pass — or at minimum exclude occurrences older than the orphaned RunningState timestamps — so post-crash missed-run detection only covers true downtime.
user_benefit: After a crash or forced reboot during the nightly window, the morning review shows an honest 'FAIL — application crashed' row instead of yesterday's success, and the 'Skipped' rows stop lying about runs that actually executed — exactly the moments when accurate history matters most.

verification.notes: Both defects trace exactly as claimed. title: while/repeat loops that hit max_iterations report success, silently truncating the run
existing_state: Both loop containers stop at max_iterations (default 10000: Services/Scripting/Commands/WhileCommand.cs:14, RepeatCommand.cs:15) and then return `new CommandResult { Success = true, ... }` after emitting only a Warning-level line (WhileCommand.cs:105-110, RepeatCommand.cs:85-90). The triggering condition is exactly the dangerous one: the `while`/`until` expression is stuck (typo'd variable name evaluating to a constant, a `send`-captured value that never changes, etc.). The script burns up to 10000 iterations of real SSH commands against the host, abandons the loop mid-work, and then continues to the following steps — and the overall run is recorded as successful in history and job results. Nothing sets _last_error, the result is not marked SuppressedError, and `on_error` has no effect since nothing failed.
recommendation: Make hitting the cap a failure by default (CommandResult.ApplyOnError with a clear message, so `on_error: continue` still allows opting out), or add an explicit `on_max_iterations: fail|continue` option on while/repeat with fail as default. At minimum set _last_error and mark the result SuppressedError so post-run checks and notifications can see the truncation.
user_benefit: A stuck loop condition surfaces as a failed step instead of a quietly truncated run that history marks green — critical when the loop is doing real work against production hosts.

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds exactly as written: cap-hit emits one Warning line then returns Success=true (WhileCommand.cs:105-110, RepeatCommand.cs:85-90, default 10000 at :14/:15), no ApplyOnError/SuppressedError/_last_error — and ScriptExecutor.cs:416-419 actually clears _last_error on the success, so the truncation is scrubbed; the run proceeds and the top level returns ScriptExitStatus.Success (ScriptExecutor.cs:245-250), recorded green in history/jobs. title: switch silently treats an invalid 'matches' regex as no-match
existing_state: A switch case written as `value: "matches <pattern>"` compiles the pattern at runtime; if the regex is invalid (typo like an unclosed paren, or a variable substituted into the pattern producing bad syntax), the bare `catch { matches = false; }` at Services/Scripting/Commands/SwitchCommand.cs:47-50 swallows the ArgumentException and the case simply never matches — no warning, no error, nothing in the output. Execution falls through to the default branch (or no-op at :83-84), so the script takes the wrong path on every host with zero diagnostics. There is also no parse-time validation of `matches` patterns in ScriptParser, so the mistake survives editing, canvas round-trips, and scheduled runs indefinitely.
recommendation: In the catch block, emit a Warning ("switch case N: invalid regex '<pattern>': <message>") via context.EmitOutput so the misroute is visible, and add a validation-time check in ScriptParser.ValidateSteps that attempts Regex construction for case values starting with 'matches ' and reports a script error before the run starts.
user_benefit: A typo in one regex no longer silently reroutes every host down the default branch — the author finds out at validation time instead of discovering wrong actions were taken fleet-wide.

evidence.note: regex branch: catch { matches = false; } with no emit — invalid pattern is indistinguishable from a legitimate non-match

verification.notes: Traced exactly as claimed: SwitchCommand.cs:42-50 swallows any regex exception with a bare catch { matches = false; }, and substitution (line 35) runs before the 'matches ' check so variable-injected bad patterns are a real trigger; ScriptParser.ValidateSteps (ScriptParser.cs:5127-5148) validates only value/case presence, never compiling the pattern. Notably, ExtractCommand.cs:108-110 already fails loudly on RegexParseException, so the silent switch behavior is an inconsistency within the same engine; ExpressionEvaluator.cs:96-103 has the same silent-catch for 'matches' in if-conditions and could be fixed alongside.

title: int()/float() return 0 on unparseable input, making 'parse failed' indistinguishable from a genuine zero in threshold logic
existing_state: TypeFunctions.ToInt returns 0 when the input cannot be parsed as a number (Services/Scripting/Functions/TypeFunctions.cs:27-46 — the final `return 0;` at line 45 covers any non-numeric string); ToFloat returns 0.0 the same way (TypeFunctions.cs:48-62). Combined with regex_match returning "" on no-match (StringFunctions.cs:197), a common monitoring pattern like `if: int(regex_match(output, "(\\d+)% used", 1)) > 90` silently evaluates to `0 > 90` = false whenever the device output format shifts — the alert branch simply never fires, on every host, with no signal. Conversely `if: int(x) == 0` fires the zero-branch on garbage input. There is no way for a script to distinguish these cases today.
recommendation: Return null on parse failure instead of 0 (the engine already handles null values distinctly throughout ValueResolver/comparison logic), and/or add an optional second argument `int(x, default)` so scripts can opt into a fallback explicitly. If backward compatibility forbids changing the return, at minimum emit a runtime warning through the step output so multi-host runs show that a conversion failed.
user_benefit: Threshold and health-check scripts are this app's bread and butter; today a format change in device output silently disables alerts fleet-wide. Distinguishing parse failure from zero makes those scripts trustworthy.

title: regex_replace() silently returns the unmodified source on an invalid pattern — sanitization/redaction steps can no-op with zero signal
existing_state: RegexReplace catches both RegexMatchTimeoutException and ArgumentException (invalid pattern) and returns the original source string unchanged (Services/Scripting/Functions/StringFunctions.cs:165-176). A script using regex_replace to strip secrets, ANSI codes, or sensitive fields from device output before logging/notifying — the docs themselves recommend a regex_replace incantation for ANSI stripping — gets the raw, unsanitized text back if the pattern has a typo or a variable-built pattern is malformed, with no error, no warning, nothing in output. regex_match has the related problem that an invalid pattern and a legitimate no-match are both "" (StringFunctions.cs:194-208), so a script cannot tell 'pattern broken' from 'value absent'.

title: iif() bare catch turns a broken condition into 'always take the then-branch'
existing_state: Iif evaluates its condition with ExpressionEvaluator inside a bare `catch` (Services/Scripting/Functions/MathFunctions.cs:184-193): when evaluation throws — e.g. `iif(lenght(x) > 0, "up", "down")` where the unknown function makes ExpressionParser throw FormatException (ExpressionParser.cs:436) — the fallback re-resolves the ENTIRE condition string as a plain value via JsonUtilities.ResolveJsonValue (MathFunctions.cs:191). That resolution falls through to the literal string "lenght(x) > 0" (per the fall-through at JsonUtilities.cs:312-333), which is non-empty and therefore truthy, so the then-branch is taken unconditionally. Any typo or evaluator error inside an iif condition thus silently pins the result to the true-value on every host, every run.
recommendation: Narrow the fallback in MathFunctions.Iif: only fall back to truthiness when the condition contains no comparison/logical operators (the legitimate 'simple value' case the comment describes); let FormatException from the evaluator propagate so the step fails with 'Unknown function: lenght'. This also becomes moot for the typo case if the unknown-function fall-through (BUG-010) is fixed.
user_benefit: iif is the branching primitive people embed in set:/send: lines; today a typo flips it into a constant. Propagating the parse error makes the failure visible at the exact step instead of producing confidently wrong branch decisions fleet-wide.

verification.notes: The symptom is real — a typo'd function in an iif condition silently yields a constant branch instead of an error — but the described mechanism is wrong. Consequently the recommended fix in MathFunctions.Iif would not change the typo behavior; the silent fallback to fix is in ExpressionEvaluator.ResolveValue/ResolveNumeric, which also affects if:/while: conditions. title: Division and modulo by zero silently return 0, propagating bad numbers into downstream decisions
existing_state: In ExpressionParser, `/` and `%` with a zero right-hand side emit a Warning line and substitute `0.0` rather than failing: `if (rhs == 0) { _context.EmitOutput("Warning: Division by zero, returning 0"...); left = 0.0; }` (ExpressionParser.cs:234-243 for `/`, 249-257 for `%`). Since denominators in this tool are frequently derived from command output (e.g. `set: pct = ${used} / ${total} * 100` where a host returns total=0), the expression yields 0 instead of erroring, and that 0 then commonly drives an `if`/threshold (`if pct > 90`) — so a host with no data is silently classified as 0% healthy and the wrong action is taken. The warning is buried in normal output and the step still reports success.
recommendation: Make divide/modulo-by-zero fail the enclosing step (throw a FormatException from ExpressionParser, which ExecuteStepCoreAsync already funnels into CommandResult.ApplyOnError), or at minimum return a sentinel that conditions treat as undefined rather than the false-but-valid value 0. If a silent default is kept for back-compat, gate it behind an explicit script option.
user_benefit: Arithmetic on missing/zero host data fails visibly instead of quietly producing 0 and steering threshold logic into the wrong branch.

evidence.note: div and mod by zero both return 0.0 with only a warning

verification.notes: Traced and confirmed: ExpressionParser.cs:230-243 (/) and 245-258 (%) substitute 0.0 on a zero denominator with only a Warning output line; SetCommand routes any expression containing '/' through this parser and still returns CommandResult.Ok(), so the step succeeds and the 0 silently feeds threshold conditions. CoerceToDouble also maps null/"0" to 0, so the missing-host-data scenario is real. One fix-design caveat: throwing FormatException from the parser alone won't work — both call sites swallow it (SetCommand.cs:191-194 falls back to raw substitution; ExpressionEvaluator.cs:337-340 catches all), so the fix needs a dedicated exception type or removal of those catches.

title: Encoding functions return wrong data instead of failing: hash() silently computes SHA256 for any unknown algorithm; hex_decode() drops the last nibble of odd-length input
existing_state: CreateHashAlgorithm's switch ends with `_ => SHA256.Create()` (Services/Scripting/Functions/EncodingFunctions.cs:104-115), so `hash(data, "crc32")` or `hash(data, "sha3-256")` returns a SHA256 digest with no error — and the intended guard `if (hasher == null) return null;` at EncodingFunctions.cs:67 is dead code because the factory can never return null. Separately, HexDecode sizes its buffer with integer division `value.Length / 2` (EncodingFunctions.cs:86-88), so an odd-length hex string like "abc" decodes only "ab" and silently discards the trailing character instead of rejecting clearly-corrupt input (the existing catch at :91-94 would have returned null had the loop been allowed to hit the bad slice).
recommendation: Change the switch default to return null so the existing null-check at line 67 does its job (hash() then returns null for unknown algorithms, consistent with base64_decode's failure behavior). In HexDecode, return null when value.Length is odd before allocating the buffer. Both are one-line fixes in EncodingFunctions.cs.
user_benefit: Scripts that verify file checksums or decode device-emitted hex get definitively wrong answers today instead of a detectable failure; a checksum comparison against the wrong algorithm fails confusingly, and truncated hex decodes pass through as plausible-looking data.

evidence.note: `_ => SHA256.Create()` — unknown algorithm silently becomes SHA256
dead null-check that the fix would reactivate
value.Length / 2 truncates the final nibble of odd-length input

verification.notes: Both behaviors verified in EncodingFunctions.cs exactly as cited: the switch default `_ => SHA256.Create()` (line 113) makes hash(data, "crc32") silently return a SHA256 digest, leaving the line-67 null-check dead, and HexDecode's `value.Length / 2` buffer (line 86) silently drops the trailing nibble of odd-length hex (e.g. "414" decodes to "A"). No upstream validation rejects unknown algorithm names or odd-length hex, the docs list only the 5 supported algorithms with no fallback contract, and the existing "xyz" test passes only by accident of "xy" being non-hex. Medium severity is right: wrong-but-silent results, triggered only by inputs outside the documented contract.

title: extract silently exports every named regex group as a script variable, clobbering existing variables of the same name
existing_state: On every successful single-match extraction, ExposeNamedGroups (Services/Scripting/Commands/ExtractCommand.cs:195-208, called from ExtractSingleMatch at 124) iterates all named groups in the pattern and calls context.SetVariable(group.Name, value) for each — unconditionally overwriting any existing variable with that name. The only trace is a Debug-level line (206) that is invisible unless debug mode is on. A pattern like `(?<host>\S+)\s+(?<status>\w+)` silently replaces the `host` / `status` variables (including CSV-column-derived variables like a `status` column) for all subsequent steps of the run, with no opt-in and no warning. Note the named group also wins even when the group didn't participate in the match (empty string overwrites the old value).
recommendation: Make named-group export opt-in (e.g. `export_groups: true` on extract, or only export groups not already present), or at minimum emit a Warning-level (not Debug) message when an existing variable is overwritten by a named group. Also skip groups that did not participate in the match (Group.Success == false) so an optional group can't blank an existing variable.
user_benefit: Stops a regex author's incidental group names from silently corrupting unrelated script state (host/credential/loop variables) mid-run — a class of failure that today is nearly undebuggable because the overwrite leaves no visible trace.

evidence.note: every non-numeric group name SetVariable'd unconditionally; only Debug-level output
ExposeNamedGroups invoked on every single-match extract before into-assignment

verification.notes: Traced fully: ExposeNamedGroups (ExtractCommand.cs:195-208, called at 124 for first/last/index modes) SetVariable's every named group with no overwrite guard (ScriptContext.SetVariable is a raw dictionary write, line 532) and no Group.Success check, so non-participating optional groups blank existing values; the Debug-level trace is suppressed entirely unless DebugMode (ScriptContext.cs:875). CSV-column variables are seeded into the same _variables store (new ScriptContext(host.Variables), SshExecutionService.cs:1542), so the claimed clobbering of e.g. a `status` column is real. One nuance: named-group export is an intentional, unit-tested feature (ExtractCommandTests.cs:218), so the bug is specifically the silent clobber + missing Success check, not the export itself — medium severity is right.

title: assert substitutes variable text into the condition before parsing — quotes/operators in data break or alter the expression (diverges from if)
existing_state: AssertCommand textually substitutes variables into the condition string and then parses the result as an expression (`context.SubstituteVariables(step.Assert.Condition)` then `evaluator.Evaluate(condition)`, Services/Scripting/Commands/AssertCommand.cs:18-24), whereas IfCommand passes the raw condition to the same ExpressionEvaluator, which resolves variable references internally (IfCommand.cs:24-28). Consequence: for `assert: '"{{output}}" contains "up"'`, any double quote, backslash, or operator-looking text in the device output is spliced into the expression source — typically producing 'Assert condition evaluation failed' (caught at 26-31, fails the step) on data that the logically identical `if:` handles fine; in unlucky cases the spliced text parses as a different expression and the assertion evaluates the wrong thing. Real device output (banners, JSON, quoted strings) hits this routinely, and the same condition string behaves differently between if and assert.
recommendation: Have AssertCommand pass step.Assert.Condition raw to ExpressionEvaluator exactly like IfCommand (delete the SubstituteVariables call at line 18; keep substitution for the `message` only). If some existing scripts rely on {{var}} splicing inside assert conditions, support both: try raw evaluation first and only fall back to substituted text when the raw parse references no resolvable form — but converging on the if semantics is the clean fix.
user_benefit: Assertions stop failing spuriously (or evaluating the wrong predicate) whenever device output contains quotes or operator characters, and if/assert finally agree on what the same condition string means.

evidence.note: substitute-then-parse; parse exception fails the step
if passes the raw condition; evaluator resolves variables itself

verification.notes: Core divergence confirmed by tracing: AssertCommand.cs:18 splices variable text into the condition before parsing, while IfCommand (and WhileCommand, which even carries a comment saying the evaluator resolves variables) pass conditions raw; the if-path is provably safe because operator splitting is quote-aware before substitution and operands substitute into values (ValueResolver.cs:266-273). Two description errors: the failure-mode weighting is inverted — ExpressionEvaluator rarely throws (inner parser errors are swallowed in try/catch), so the typical outcome is a silently wrong boolean (including a should-fail assert passing on odd quote counts), not the "Assert condition evaluation failed" error the finding calls typical; and the trigger is narrower than "routinely" — only {{var}}/${var}-style conditions are exposed, while every documented assert example uses bare variable names, which behave identically in if and assert. Medium severity still fits.

title: input validate regex runs with no timeout on the UI thread — a pathological pattern freezes the whole app
existing_state: InputCommand compiles the user-supplied `validate:` pattern with `new Regex(step.Input.Validate, RegexOptions.Compiled)` and no match timeout (Services/Scripting/Commands/InputCommand.cs:41). The match executes in the dialog's OK handler on the UI thread (`_validationRegex.IsMatch(_txtInput.Text)` in BtnOk_Click, InputCommand.cs:209). A backtracking-prone pattern (e.g. `^(\w+\s?)*$`) combined with a longish non-matching input hangs the entire WinForms message pump indefinitely — no Stop button, no recovery except killing the process. The codebase already has the fix pattern: ScriptRegexDefaults.UserPatternTimeout (5s, Services/Scripting/ScriptRegexDefaults.cs:10) is used for the same class of user-authored patterns in ExtractCommand.cs:60 and ExpressionEvaluator.cs:98 — input validation is the one place it was missed.
recommendation: Pass ScriptRegexDefaults.UserPatternTimeout as the third Regex constructor argument at InputCommand.cs:41, and catch RegexMatchTimeoutException in BtnOk_Click (treat as validation failure with a 'pattern timed out' message). Optionally drop RegexOptions.Compiled, which buys nothing for a few interactive matches.
user_benefit: A typo'd validation regex in a script can no longer hard-freeze the app mid-fleet-run at an interactive prompt, taking the unsent work of the whole run with it.

evidence.note: Regex compiled without timeout
IsMatch on the UI thread in BtnOk_Click
5s UserPatternTimeout exists and is used by extract and the expression evaluator

verification.notes: Traced fully: the validate regex is compiled with no timeout (InputCommand.cs:41, no process-wide regex timeout set anywhere), and IsMatch runs in BtnOk_Click on the main UI message pump (dialog is shown modeless on the main form's thread via ScriptPromptDialogRunner). During a backtracking hang the Stop button and the cancellation-close path are both unreachable (both need the blocked pump), so only killing the process recovers. ExtractCommand.cs:60 and ExpressionEvaluator.cs:98 do use the 5s UserPatternTimeout as claimed; one nit — SwitchCommand.cs:44 also lacks the timeout (executor thread, not UI), so "the one place missed" is slightly overstated but InputCommand is indeed the only UI-freezing instance.

title: Retry loop mutates the shared step.OnError field; concurrent parallel/subroutine reuse of a step races
existing_state: The retry path temporarily rewrites the step object's OnError and restores it in a finally: `var originalOnError = step.OnError; ... step.OnError = onErrorForAttempt; try { ... } finally { step.OnError = originalOnError; }` (ScriptExecutor.cs:456-471). ScriptStep instances are not per-execution copies — subroutine bodies are parsed once and the same `ScriptSubroutineDefinition.Subroutine.Steps` instances are executed every call. ParallelCommand runs each branch on the shared context concurrently via Task.Run (ParallelCommand.cs:40-61) with the comment 'Steps share one context'. So if two parallel branches both `call:` the same subroutine (or a parallel branch and the main flow re-enter the same shared step) and that step has `retry:`, the two executions write/restore the same `step.OnError` without synchronization — one branch can permanently observe the other's forced 'stop', or have its original on_error wiped to the interleaved value, changing whether failures are suppressed. The same shared-instance hazard touches `step.StepPath ??=` (ScriptExecutor.cs:318), though that one is idempotent.
recommendation: Stop mutating shared step state for retry: thread the per-attempt on_error override as a parameter into ExecuteStepCoreAsync / the command result evaluation instead of writing step.OnError, so retry attempts never touch the shared ScriptStep. This also makes retries safe under Parallel and concurrent subroutine calls.
user_benefit: Retries inside parallel blocks or shared subroutines behave deterministically instead of intermittently flipping error-handling behavior under concurrency.

evidence.note: retry mutates and restores shared step.OnError
branches run concurrently on the shared context/steps

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end: the retry loop (ScriptExecutor.cs:456-471) mutates the shared step.OnError with no synchronization; subroutine bodies execute the same parsed ScriptStep instances on every call (ExecuteSubroutineAsync runs definition.Subroutine.Steps directly, line 656; no clone path exists), and ParallelCommand runs branches concurrently via Task.Run. Commands read step.OnError mid-execution (CallCommand, ReadFile/WriteFile, IScriptCommand defaults), and the save/restore interleave can permanently leave "stop" on the step for the rest of the run — so two parallel branches calling the same retry-bearing subroutine do race exactly as claimed. Only nit: "main flow re-enters the same shared step" concurrently can't happen (main flow blocks on Task.WhenAll); the parallel-branches-into-shared-subroutine scenario is the real trigger, which the finding leads with.

title: Capture-mode 'natural completion' can fire early on prompt-like output, killing the still-running remote command
existing_state: Capture mode (interactive with `command:`) decides the command is finished per received chunk: after dispatch, `ShouldArmCaptureNaturalCompletion` arms on the first chunk that contains the command text as a case-insensitive substring of any line (Services/Terminal/InteractiveTerminalService.cs:2690-2712) OR simply isn't prompt-terminated (2674-2683) — i.e., effectively any output arms it. Completion then triggers when the last non-empty line of a chunk matches the detected prompt regex, falling back to `PromptDetector.IsLikelyPrompt` heuristics when startup prompt detection failed (2714-2734; call sites 800-814 windowed, 1390-1404 headless). Chunk boundaries are arbitrary network reads, so a mid-output chunk ending on a prompt-looking line (device status dumps echoing `hostname #`, log lines ending in `$`/`>`, cat of a session log) completes the capture early. On `natural_complete` the step returns Ok with the truncated transcript (563) and the `finally` block disconnects the separate SSH session (573-575) — terminating the still-running remote command (the canonical use case is long-running operations like upgrades), while the step and any `capture:` variable report success.
recommendation: Make completion stricter: require the prompt match to be anchored at the true end of accumulated output (carry an incomplete-final-line buffer like the transcript path already does, rather than testing each raw chunk), require the detected prompt regex when available instead of `IsLikelyPrompt`, and debounce — confirm the prompt persists across a short quiet window (e.g. 300-500 ms with no further output) before declaring `natural_complete`. Keep `max_seconds`/`max_lines` as the hard caps.
user_benefit: Prevents the worst capture failure mode: a long-running command (firmware upgrade, migration) being SIGHUP-killed mid-flight because its own output happened to look like a prompt, while the script reports the step as successfully completed with a truncated transcript.

evidence.note: arming returns true for any non-prompt chunk or any line containing the command substring
case-insensitive substring echo match; completion tests only the last line of the current chunk; IsLikelyPrompt fallback
per-chunk arm/complete in both windowed and headless capture loops
natural_complete returns Ok; finally disconnects the session, killing the remote command

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: capture completion tests only the last non-empty line of each raw DataReceived chunk (no accumulated-buffer anchoring, no debounce), so a mid-output chunk ending on a prompt-shaped line fires natural_complete; the step returns Ok, capture: stores the truncated transcript, and the finally disconnects the dedicated session, killing the still-running command. It is slightly worse than written: even the "detected prompt" regex (BuildPromptRegex) matches anchor + anything + any of #>$% (with a match-any-terminator fallback regex for non-terminator literals), so hostname-prefixed output lines ending in a terminator also complete early. Existing unit tests validate the per-chunk design but none cover prompt-mimicking output at a chunk boundary; all cited line numbers are accurate.

title: Opening or resizing a shared-session terminal window permanently rewrites the pooled shell's geometry
existing_state: In `session: shared` mode the window is bound to the pooled script session's live terminal (`sharedSession.SharedTerminal`, Services/Terminal/InteractiveTerminalService.cs:285 and 294-295; SshShellSession.cs:115 exposes `_scripting.Terminal`). `InteractiveTerminalForm.OnShown` immediately fires `EmitTerminalSizeChanged` (Forms/InteractiveTerminalForm.cs:216-221), which computes columns/rows from the window's pixel client size (339-364), and the handler calls `terminal.SetScreenSize(...)` on that pooled terminal (InteractiveTerminalService.cs:1843-1859). The pooled session was created at 120x36 (Services/SshTerminalOptionsFactory.cs:13-14), so merely opening the window — and certainly any user resize — changes the remote PTY geometry, and nothing restores it after the window closes: `SyncAfterInteractive` only sends \r and re-reads to the prompt (Services/SshShellSession.cs:344-365). Every subsequent `send`/`expect` step in the same script then runs against the altered width, changing line wrapping and pager trigger points — which is exactly what the prompt/pager regexes and `TerminalOutputProcessor` line handling key off.
recommendation: Capture the pooled terminal's columns/rows before handing it to `RunWindowLoopAsync` in `RunSharedAsync`, and restore them (inside the same `ioLock`) right before `SyncAfterInteractive()` in the close path. Alternatively, in shared mode render at the session's existing geometry and ignore window-driven `TerminalSizeChanged` (letterbox the viewport) so the script session is never perturbed.
user_benefit: Stops a class of 'script worked until I peeked at it' failures: today a quick shared-mode look at a session can change output wrapping for the rest of the run, breaking expect patterns and pager handling in ways that look like random flakiness.

evidence.note: shared mode binds the window to the pooled session's SharedTerminal
OnShown emits TerminalSizeChanged computed from window pixels
handler calls SetScreenSize on the pooled terminal; nothing saves/restores
SyncAfterInteractive realigns the prompt only — no geometry restore
pooled session default geometry 120x36

verification.notes: Fully traced and accurate. Shared mode hands the pooled session's live VirtualTerminal to the window loop; the form opens at a fixed 980x620 (shared mode passes no initialColumns/initialRows, unlike separate mode), OnShown always fires the first TerminalSizeChanged (dedupe fields start at 0), and the handler calls SetScreenSize with window-derived geometry (~118 cols, not 120x36) — so even opening without resizing perturbs the PTY. Grep confirms no restore site exists; SyncAfterInteractive only realigns the prompt. One minor scoping note: "permanently" lasts only for that session lease — the pool recreates a fresh 120x36 terminal per CreateSessionAsync, so the damage is confined to the remainder of the same script run, exactly as the finding body states.

title: Shared-session exit/logout guard is trivially bypassed, killing the pooled shell mid-script while the step reports success
existing_state: In shared mode, typing `exit`/`logout` is supposed to detach the window instead of terminating the pooled shell the rest of the script depends on. But `ShouldBlockSharedShellCommand` matches only the exact trimmed strings "exit" and "logout" (Services/Terminal/InteractiveTerminalService.cs:2952-2960), and the guard's local line buffer resets to empty on any navigation/control key (3160-3165, with a comment acknowledging it). So `exit 0`, `exit;`, `;exit`, or pressing an arrow key before typing `exit` all reach the host and terminate the shared shell. The disconnect then closes the window with reason `disconnected`, which `RunSharedAsync` still returns as success (line 310, see BUG-030), and every subsequent SSH step in the script fails against the dead pooled session with unrelated-looking connection errors. `SyncAfterInteractive` no-ops because the client is no longer connected (SshShellSession.cs:346-347).
recommendation: Stop trying to reconstruct the command line client-side. Either (a) extend the match to a regex like ^\s*(exit|logout)\b on the buffer and additionally treat shared-mode shell termination as a step failure with a clear message ('shared session terminated from interactive window'), or (b) accept the bypass but detect the shared session's death on window close (sharedSession.IsConnected) and fail/flag the step there so the run stops with an accurate error instead of cascading confusing failures.
user_benefit: A user habitually typing `exit 0` in the shared window currently nukes the script's SSH session and gets a wall of misleading errors from later steps; this makes the failure immediate, accurate, and attributable.

evidence.note: exact-match exit/logout only
guard buffer resets on any nav/control key — acknowledged in comment
shared window closing as 'disconnected' still returns Ok to the script step
SyncAfterInteractive silently no-ops once the shared client is dead

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: the guard matches only exact trimmed "exit"/"logout" (InteractiveTerminalService.cs:2952-2960), so "exit 0"/"exit;" kill the shared shell; the disconnect closes the window as 'disconnected' yet RunSharedAsync line 310 returns Ok and InteractiveCommand reports the step successful; SyncAfterInteractive no-ops (SshShellSession.cs:346-347) and later sends throw "SSH connection was closed unexpectedly" (SshShellSession.cs:755-758) with no reconnect mid-script. Two trigger examples are slightly off: an arrow key BEFORE typing exit is actually still blocked (the buffer rebuilds from typed text) — the real nav-key bypass is arrow AFTER typing or up-arrow history recall of "exit"; and ";exit" bypasses the guard but is a bash syntax error so it usually won't terminate the shell. Neither error changes scope or fix; medium severity is right.

title: FlushBuffer / DrainResidualBuffer loop forever on a continuously-streaming device (no iteration cap, no cancellation)
existing_state: `FlushBuffer` (`SshShellSession.cs:317-339`) and `DrainResidualBuffer` (`:1393-1415`) both loop `while (true) { _stream.ReadData(); }` and rely *solely* on a read-timeout exception to terminate — FlushBuffer with a 200ms window, DrainResidualBuffer with a 25ms window — with no maximum iteration count and no `CancellationToken` check inside the loop. If the remote device emits output continuously faster than that window (e.g. a session where `top`/`tail -f`/a chatty MOTD or background logging keeps writing to the TTY), `ReadData()` keeps returning data and never throws a timeout, so the loop never exits. Both are on common paths: `FlushBuffer` runs after init on the non-pooled simple-command path (`SshExecutionService.cs:2270`), and `DrainResidualBuffer` runs before *every* command send. Because the loop ignores the cancellation token, the user's Stop button cannot break it, and the whole run hangs.
recommendation: Bound both loops: add a max-iterations / max-wall-clock cap (e.g. drain for at most a few hundred ms total or N reads) and check `cancellationToken`/the session's CT inside the loop, breaking out when exceeded. Thread the execution CancellationToken into `DrainResidualBuffer` and `FlushBuffer` so Stop can interrupt them.
user_benefit: Prevents the app from hanging indefinitely (un-cancellable) when a host streams output, instead of silently locking up the run.

evidence.note: FlushBuffer while(true) ReadData with only a timeout exit, no cap/CT
DrainResidualBuffer same unbounded pattern, runs before every send
FlushBuffer called on the common non-pooled command path

verification.notes: Traced and confirmed. Both loops are unbounded while(true) ReadData() with no iteration/wall-clock cap and no CancellationToken check; ReadData (IShellStream.cs:63 = Rebex Scripting.ReadUntil(AnyData)) returns whenever any data arrives, so a device streaming with gaps under the 200ms/25ms quiet window never lets the loop exit. DrainResidualBuffer runs before every send (lines 543/580/621) and FlushBuffer at SshExecutionService.cs:2270 as cited. Stop() only cancels the CTS without disconnecting, so it cannot interrupt the loop — only a connection drop can. One minor nit: DrainResidualBuffer also breaks on an empty read (lines 1402-1403), so it doesn't rely "solely" on the timeout exception, but that branch never fires on a streaming device, so the conclusion is unaffected.

title: Vault KV-version auto-detect defaults to V2 on a double-404, breaking restricted KV v1 mounts
existing_state: When KvVersion is AutoDetect and the sys/mounts/{mount}/tune probe is forbidden or inconclusive, DetectKvVersionByHeuristicAsync probes `v1/{mount}/data/detect-kv-version-probe` then `v1/{mount}/detect-kv-version-probe`; if BOTH return 404 it unconditionally sets DetectedKvVersion = V2 (Services/Vault/VaultService.cs:664-665). For a genuine KV v1 mount whose policy does not grant the probe path (or simply has no such secret), both probes legitimately return 404, so the mount is then driven with V2 `data/`-prefixed read/write/list URLs (e.g. WriteSecretAsync VaultService.cs:160-168, ListSecretsAsync :204-207). Every subsequent operation fails or returns a misleading 'No secret found', and the user has no obvious way to know the version was guessed wrong.
recommendation: On a double-404, do not silently assume V2. Prefer surfacing an explicit, actionable VaultException ('could not auto-detect KV version for mount X — set KV version explicitly in the profile') so the operator pins V1/V2 in Settings, or weight the heuristic by the mount's behavior (e.g. a 404 with a Vault-style errors body vs a routing 404). At minimum, document that AutoDetect is unreliable for locked-down v1 mounts and make the Settings KV-version dropdown default to an explicit choice.
user_benefit: KV v1 users with least-privilege policies stop getting silent, misleading 'No secret found' failures and instead get a clear instruction to pin the KV version.

evidence.note: both-404 path defaults to V2
V2 assumption injects data/ prefix into write URL

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end: with KvVersion=AutoDetect (the default) and the sys/mounts tune probe forbidden, a double-404 on the probe paths unconditionally sets DetectedKvVersion=V2 (VaultService.cs:664-665); all subsequent ops then use data//metadata/ URLs (162/205/678/716/782) which 404 on a real v1 mount and are translated to the misleading "No secret found" message (987-989), with no self-correction or user-visible detected version. Minor nit: a policy-denied probe actually returns 403, not 404, which trips the v2Code!=404 branch at line 634 and mis-detects V2 even earlier — so the bug is slightly broader than described; the double-404 case applies to any v1 mount where the probe secret simply doesn't exist (essentially always). Medium severity is right: pinning v1 explicitly in Settings is a working escape hatch. [updated refs: Services/Vault/VaultService.cs:624-666 (heuristic, both-404 default at 664-665); :160-168 (V2 write URL); also relevant: :310 (detection on every auth), :204-207 (list metadata/ URL), :987-989 (404 → "No secret found" translation), Models/VaultSettings.cs:125 (AutoDetect default)]

title: Running a folder silently excludes presets inside its subfolders
existing_state: ExecuteFolderPresetsAsync builds the run list via GetSortedPresetsInFolder (Form1.cs:12836-12837), which calls PresetManager.GetPresetsInFolder — an exact ordinal match on the folder path (Services/PresetManager.cs:762-769). Presets in nested subfolders are never included; the FolderExecutionDialog (Form1.cs:12850) simply lists the direct children, so nothing tells the user that 'Datacenter/Switches' presets were left out of a 'Datacenter' run. The app is inconsistent about folder semantics: deleting the same folder counts and operates on all descendants (CountPresetsInFolderAndDescendants, Form1.cs:8124-8126).
recommendation: Include descendant presets in the folder-run preset list (grouped/prefixed by subfolder path in FolderExecutionDialog so users can uncheck whole subfolders), or at minimum show an explicit note in the dialog when N presets in subfolders were excluded. Whichever semantic is chosen, align it with the delete-folder behavior.
user_benefit: Operators who organize presets hierarchically and run a parent folder currently get a partial run that reports success — the missing subfolder presets are easy to overlook in the dialog and there is no warning anywhere.
mockup_idea: Before/after of FolderExecutionDialog: before shows a flat list of 3 direct-child presets for 'Datacenter'; after shows the same plus a 'Switches/' group with its 4 presets indented and checkable, with a count line 'Includes 4 presets from 1 subfolder'.

evidence.note: Run list = GetSortedPresetsInFolder, dialog shows only that list
Exact-folder ordinal match; no descendants
Folder delete counts descendants — inconsistent semantics

verification.notes: Traced fully: ExecuteFolderPresetsAsync (Form1.cs:12837) -> GetSortedPresetsInFolder (11123) -> PresetManager.GetPresetsInFolder (762-769), which matches the folder path with strict ordinal equality, so nested-subfolder presets are silently excluded from folder runs; FolderExecutionDialog only renders the flat list it is given with no exclusion notice (a parent with presets only in subfolders even reports "contains no presets"). Folder delete meanwhile uses CountPresetsInFolderAndDescendants (Form1.cs:8125, PresetManager.cs:815-820), confirming the inconsistent semantics. Medium is right since the dialog does show exactly which presets will run, so the omission is visible to a careful user but never flagged.

title: Connection tests cannot be cancelled once started
existing_state: TestSelectedConnections creates `_connectionTestCts` and handles OperationCanceledException (Form1.cs:8899-8900, 8949-8953), but a repo-wide search shows no code path ever calls `.Cancel()` — the CTS is only created (8899) and disposed (8958-8959). With all checked rows tested at `config.ConnectionTimeout` seconds each, capped to 5 concurrent (SemaphoreSlim(5), 8910), a fleet of unreachable hosts means e.g. 200 hosts x 10s / 5 = ~7 minutes of unstoppable 'Testing...' overlays, during which `_isTestingConnections` (8877) blocks starting another test, and the main Stop button only stops `_sshService` (StopExecution, Form1.cs:13282-13299), not this run.
recommendation: Wire a cancel affordance: morph the status-bar progress area (or grid context menu) into 'Cancel test' while `_isTestingConnections` is true and have it call `_connectionTestCts.Cancel()`; pass the token's cancellation into the per-row visual cleanup so stuck 'Testing...' overlays are cleared. Also guard the result paint at 8935 with the same `hostIpColIndex >= 0` check used at 8922.
user_benefit: Accidentally testing a large checked set against a dead network segment currently locks the feature for minutes with no way out except waiting or killing the app.

evidence.note: CTS created/disposed, OCE handled, but no Cancel() call exists anywhere (verified by repo-wide grep of _connectionTestCts)
StopExecution only stops _sshService, not connection tests

verification.notes: Verified end-to-end: _connectionTestCts is only created (Form1.cs:8899) and disposed (8958-8959) — repo-wide grep shows no .Cancel() path; _isTestingConnections (8877/8898/8957) blocks restarting; StopExecution (13282-13299) early-returns unless _sshService.IsRunning and only stops _sshService. The claim is conservative: ConnectionTimeout defaults to 30s (not the cited 10s example), so 200 dead hosts / 5 concurrent is ~20 minutes unstoppable. One nit: the recommendation's secondary item (guard the result paint at 8935) is already handled — ApplyConnectionTestCellResult self-guards hostIpColIndex < 0 at Form1.cs:2749; the cancel-affordance fix itself is still needed and the token already threads correctly into TestConnectionAsync and the semaphore wait.

title: Cancelling the import-destination prompt imports all presets to root level anyway
existing_state: ImportAllPresets asks for a destination via PromptForImportDestination (Form1.cs:10804). If the user answers Yes ('choose a folder') and then presses Cancel on the VB InputBox, the empty return is indistinguishable from 'leave empty for root' — the code comment admits this (Form1.cs:10880-10885) and returns the empty string, so the import proceeds dumping every preset at root level (10810) with '_imported' suffixes on collisions. The bulk import then clears the preset-delete undo history (10824), and there is no import-undo, so cleanup of a bad import is fully manual. A proper wrapper already exists (`ShowInputBox`, Form1.cs:11304 area, with test seam) but this call site uses `Microsoft.VisualBasic.Interaction.InputBox` directly (10875).
recommendation: Replace the VB InputBox with a small themed dialog (or extend ShowInputBox) that returns a real cancelled/ok result plus the text — e.g. a folder picker combo seeded from _presetManager.GetFolders() with OK/Cancel — and abort the import on cancel. Same fix applies to the other three direct InputBox call sites (8093, 9391, 9419).
user_benefit: Pressing Cancel should never mutate the preset library; today it can flood the root level with dozens of imported presets that must be cleaned up one by one (and it wipes the delete-undo stack in the process).

evidence.note: Cancel/empty ambiguity acknowledged in comment; empty returned as 'import to root'
Only the first dialog's ESC sentinel aborts; import proceeds and clears undo history

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end: Yes on the destination prompt then Cancel on the VB InputBox returns "" (Form1.cs:10875-10885, ambiguity admitted in the comment), which ImportAllPresets treats as "import to root" (10810) — PresetManager.ImportAllFromFile clears each preset's Folder for empty targetFolder (PresetManager.cs:475-479), suffixes collisions with "_imported" (469), and the import then wipes the delete-undo stack (10824) with no import-undo anywhere. The cited ShowInputBox wrapper (11304) and the three other direct InputBox sites (8093, 9391, 9419) are exactly where claimed; note ShowInputBox also can't signal cancel today, so the fix must extend it as the recommendation says. Medium severity is right: cancel-mutates-state is a nasty surprise but nothing is overwritten or lost.

title: EnvironmentDialog Save swallows all persistence failures and closes as if it succeeded
existing_state: PersistCurrentEnvironmentDetails wraps the only write of description/color/variables/vault-binding in a bare `catch { }` (EnvironmentDialog.cs:807-823) — the comment claims "actionable errors are shown on explicit operations," but the explicit Save button routes through this exact method (BtnSave_Click, 639-643) and the button carries DialogResult.OK (249), so the form closes successfully even when ConfigurationService.SaveEnvironmentState threw (config.json locked by AV/backup tooling, disk full, KeyNotFoundException from UpdateEnvironmentDetails at Services/EnvironmentService.cs:311-312). Every variable the user just entered is silently discarded while the UI reports success and Form1 proceeds to switch environments.
recommendation: Split the behavior: keep the silent catch for the high-frequency selection-change autosave, but have BtnSave_Click call a throwing variant — on exception, show a DialogTheme.Show error and set `DialogResult = DialogResult.None` so the dialog stays open and the user's grid contents are not lost.
user_benefit: A failed disk write no longer eats an entire environment-variable editing session without a word — the user gets a chance to retry or copy their data out.

evidence.note: catch-all with no logging or surfacing
Save routes through the swallowing method; button's DialogResult.OK closes the form regardless

verification.notes: Traced fully: BtnSave_Click (EnvironmentDialog.cs:639-643) routes through PersistCurrentEnvironmentDetails whose bare catch (819-822) swallows everything, and ConfigurationService.Save explicitly rethrows disk-write failures as InvalidOperationException (ConfigurationService.cs:147-150), so the failure genuinely reaches and dies in that catch. The OK-DialogResult button (line 249) then closes the dialog and Form1 (1941-1954) proceeds to switch environments — exactly as claimed. No throwing variant exists; medium severity is appropriate since the loss only occurs on a failure path.

title: Notifications tab: clicking Add silently discards all unsaved edits (including a just-typed password) on the currently selected profile
existing_state: BtnNotificationAdd_Click (SettingsDialog.cs:1424-1440) creates the new profile, suppresses selection events (_suppressNotificationProfileSelection = true at 1429), selects the new row, and overwrites _activeNotificationProfileIndex (1433) — without ever calling PersistCurrentNotificationProfile. Because the selection-change handler that normally flushes edits (1396-1401) is suppressed, everything the user typed into the previously selected profile (SMTP host/port/recipients, webhook URL, SMTP password, rename) is lost the moment they click Add. evidence.note: No persist call; selection events suppressed; active index overwritten
Vault Add shows the correct pattern: PersistCurrentVaultProfile() first
