title: Duplicate profile names are trivially created (profile-N collision) and duplicated profiles silently share one credential-store slot
existing_state: Both Add buttons generate names as `profile-{Count + 1}` (SettingsDialog.cs:821 vault, 1426 notifications). Sequence: Add, Add (profile-1, profile-2), remove profile-1, Add -> Count is 1 so the new profile is also named "profile-2". Nothing prevents typing a duplicate name either: ValidateVaultProfiles only checks for empty names (2762-2768) and notifications have no name validation at all. Two same-named profiles read and write the identical CredentialTargets target — selecting one and letting persist fire (1011-1017 / 1577-1581) overwrites the other profile's token/webhook/password with no warning, and default-profile resolution picks whichever matches first (1169-1171, 1685-1687). The user ends up with two visually distinct profiles whose secrets clobber each other.
recommendation: Generate unique names by scanning existing names (e.g. increment until `profile-N` is free), and add a duplicate-name check (OrdinalIgnoreCase, matching the lookup semantics used everywhere) to ValidateVaultProfiles plus an equivalent notification validation before SaveNotificationSettings — block Save with a themed prompt naming the collision.
user_benefit: Prevents two profiles from invisibly sharing and corrupting each other's stored secrets, and removes an ambiguity that also confuses default-profile resolution.

evidence.note: Name = profile-{Count+1}; collides after any deletion
Validation checks only IsNullOrWhiteSpace(Name); no duplicate guard; notifications validate nothing
Same-named profiles write the same VaultAuthTarget; default resolution takes first name match

verification.notes: Traced every cited site and the claim holds exactly: both Add buttons use Count+1 naming (821, 1426) so remove+add reproduces a duplicate name; ValidateVaultProfiles (2762-2768) only rejects empty names, notifications have no name validation at all, and credential targets are name-keyed ({prefix}:vault:{name}:{type}), so duplicates share one slot and persist (1011-1017 / 1577-1581) silently overwrites. The finding even understates it: removing one duplicate deletes the survivor's secrets too (854-857, 1453-1454), and the notification rename migration (1584-1593) moves-and-deletes by old name, stealing the other duplicate's secret.

title: Run Now is an async-void handler with no try/catch over code paths that perform throwing disk writes
existing_state: OnRunNowClick (JobListDialog.cs:1061-1076) is async void with no try/catch; it awaits RunNowJobAsync (JobListDialog.cs:1515-1523), which in production routes to Form1.RunTrackedJobNowAsync (Form1.cs:15311-15326, also no try/catch) and then JobExecutionService.RunNowAsync. RunNowAsync's own catch blocks only cover ExecuteTrackedJobAsync — but its start path TryStartJob persists RunningState via _jobStorage.Save (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:768-774), its finally path CompleteJob also calls _jobStorage.Save (827-832), and the exception handlers themselves call HandlePostExecution which can call Save (251, 258 -> 877-888). JobStorageService.PersistToDisk does real file I/O on jobs.json, so a locked file, disk-full, or AV interference throws straight through the awaited chain into the async-void continuation on the UI thread. The repo registers no Application.ThreadException / AppDomain.UnhandledException handler anywhere (see BUG-037), so the user gets the raw WinForms unhandled-exception dialog — or process termination — instead of an error message, while the job may actually be mid-run.
recommendation: Wrap the body of OnRunNowClick in try/catch and surface failures via the existing DialogTheme.Show error pattern used by every sibling handler (e.g. OnNewClick at JobListDialog.cs:1043-1052). Defense in depth: have RunNowAsync catch persistence failures from TryStartJob/CompleteJob (RunningState persistence is best-effort crash-recovery metadata — a failed write should log and continue, not abort/crash the run).
user_benefit: A transient jobs.json write failure during Run Now degrades to a readable error message instead of crashing the whole application mid-fleet-run.

evidence.note: async void handler with no try/catch, unlike every neighboring handler
TryStartJob and CompleteJob (finally) perform _jobStorage.Save outside the catch coverage; HandlePostExecution Saves inside the catch blocks
RunTrackedJobNowAsync passes exceptions through; no global ThreadException/UnhandledException handler exists in the repo

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and the claim holds: OnRunNowClick is async void with no try/catch, Form1.RunTrackedJobNowAsync passes exceptions through, and RunNowAsync calls _jobStorage.Save both before its try block (TryStartJob, line 773) and in its finally (CompleteJob, line 831) — PersistToDisk ends in a bare File.WriteAllText, and no ThreadException/UnhandledException handler exists anywhere in the repo, so an I/O failure surfaces as the raw WinForms unhandled-exception dialog. One minor inaccuracy: the HandlePostExecution-inside-catch Save paths (lines 880/887) are unreachable for Run Now (they require success=true or isRunNow=false), but the two primary throw points fully support the finding and the recommendation stands. [updated refs: JobStorageService.PersistToDisk unguarded write is Services/JobStorageService.cs:227-244 (File.WriteAllText at :243); all other cited refs are exact as of 0.51.23]

title: UpdateDialog: retrying a failed download detaches the progress handler, showing a frozen bar that invites the user to kill a healthy download
existing_state: On a retryable download error, the catch block unsubscribes DownloadProgressChanged and re-invokes BtnYes_Click directly (UpdateDialog.cs:643-645). BtnYes_Click is `async void`, so the recursive call returns to the caller at its first await (the DownloadUpdateAsync await at 536) right after re-subscribing the handler at 525 — and then the OUTER invocation's `finally` runs (660-663) and unsubscribes the handler the retry just registered. The retried download proceeds with the bar stuck at 0% under "Downloading update..." with no byte counts. Because UpdateDialog_FormClosing cancels the download CTS (457-460), a user who concludes the update hung and closes the dialog aborts a download that was actually progressing fine.
recommendation: Replace the recursive re-invocation with a loop: wrap the download/verify/install body in `while (true) { try { ... break; } catch (retryable) { if (user declines) break; } }` with subscribe/unsubscribe hoisted outside the loop — or simply move the subscribe into the try and skip the recursion by extracting the body into a private async Task method awaited in a loop.
user_benefit: Retried update downloads show real progress instead of appearing hung, so users stop cancelling working updates.

evidence.note: Recursive async-void call at 644; outer finally at 662 unsubscribes the handler the inner call subscribed at 525
Closing the seemingly-frozen dialog cancels the CTS and aborts the in-flight retry

verification.notes: Traced and confirmed exactly as described. The retry path (UpdateDialog.cs:640-645) calls the async-void BtnYes_Click recursively; the inner call re-subscribes DownloadProgressChanged at 525 and yields at the await (536), after which the outer invocation's finally (660-663) detaches that fresh subscription. UpdateDownloadProgress (688-695) is the only code updating the bar/byte text, so the retried download runs frozen at 0% under "Downloading update...", and FormClosing (457-460) cancels the retry's CTS — closing the seemingly-hung dialog aborts a healthy download. The bug repeats at every retry depth; medium severity is appropriate since the update still completes if the user waits.

title: Corrupt history index orphans every run payload and the next index write clobbers the good index backup
existing_state: history.index.json is written atomically WITH a .bak (Services/HistoryStorageService.cs:609-613 -> JsonFileWriter.WriteJsonAtomic createBackup:true), but ReadIndexDocument never uses that backup: on a parse failure it copies the corrupt file to a timestamped .corrupt (HistoryStorageService.cs:602-606, :736-737 — copy, not move, so the corrupt file stays at the index path) and returns a fresh empty index. Two consequences: (1) all history/{id}.json payloads remain on disk but become permanently invisible — nothing rescans the run folder (only DeleteAll sweeps it, :518-524); (2) the next index write — which happens on the very next run save or delete — calls File.Replace(temp, index, index.bak) (Utilities/JsonFileWriter.cs:40), moving the still-corrupt index over the last good .bak, destroying the only file that could have restored the list. Per-run load failures are also indistinguishable: TryLoadRunPayload swallows every exception into `return false` (:92-96), so locked vs corrupt vs missing all render as the same generic failure.
recommendation: In ReadIndexDocument's catch: first try history.index.json.bak before resetting to empty, and back up the corrupt file with useMove:true so it can't be re-promoted into .bak. Add an orphan-reconciliation pass (on empty-index load, scan history/*.json and rebuild entries from payload Id + file mtime — ParseCreatedAtUtc already exists for label-derived timestamps). Optionally log the swallowed exception in TryLoadRunPayload so locked-file vs corrupt-file failures are diagnosable.
user_benefit: One corrupted index file no longer silently erases the entire execution-history list while the data still sits on disk unrecoverable.

evidence.note: corrupt index -> .corrupt copy + empty index; .bak written but never read
File.Replace promotes the still-corrupt index into .bak on next write
exception-swallowing payload load; only DeleteAll ever sweeps orphans

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end and accurate. ReadIndexDocument's catch (HistoryStorageService.cs:602-606) copies (not moves — TryBackupCorrupt useMove defaults false, JsonFileWriter.cs:117) the corrupt index to a timestamped .corrupt and returns an empty index; the next index write (SaveRun/DeleteRun/DeleteAll/ImportLegacy all call WriteIndexDocument) runs File.Replace (JsonFileWriter.cs:40) which promotes the still-corrupt file into .bak, destroying the only good backup — and nothing in the codebase ever reads history.index.json.bak. Payloads in history/ become permanently invisible: the only run-folder scan is DeleteAll's delete sweep (:518-524), and EnforceRetention only touches indexed entries, so orphans persist forever. TryLoadRunPayload's blanket catch (:92-96) is also as described. Medium severity is right: the trigger needs externally-caused index corruption (the app's own writes are atomic) and payloads remain recoverable on disk.

title: CSV load rejects files with duplicate headers and silently drops cells from over-long rows (loss becomes permanent on save-back)
existing_state: Two robustness gaps in CsvManager.LoadFromFile: (1) duplicate column names — common in spreadsheet exports, and including the case where any later column is literally named "Host_IP" (the first header is unconditionally discarded and replaced with Host_IP at Services/CsvManager.cs:32-35) — make `dt.Columns.Add(headerName)` (:46) throw DuplicateNameException, surfaced as a raw "Failed to load CSV: A column named 'X' already belongs to this DataTable" dialog (Form1.cs:9239-9242); the file cannot be opened at all. Note headers also collapse via the space->underscore rewrite (:45), so "port 1" and "port_1" collide. (2) Rows with more cells than the header are truncated without any warning (Array.Resize at :61-62); because saving writes the grid back over the same file (Form1.cs:9285-9325), one load-then-save round trip permanently deletes the extra columns' data from the user's file.
recommendation: In LoadFromFile: deduplicate header names deterministically (append _2, _3...) instead of letting DataTable throw, treat a non-first "Host_IP" header the same way, and count truncated rows — return or expose a load summary so Form1 can show "N rows had extra fields that were ignored" before the user saves over the original.
user_benefit: Real-world spreadsheet exports load instead of erroring, and a quiet open/save cycle can no longer permanently strip data out of the operator's hosts file.

evidence.note: first header discarded -> Host_IP; dt.Columns.Add throws on duplicates
silent Array.Resize truncation of over-long rows
raw DuplicateNameException message shown; load aborted

verification.notes: Both claims trace exactly. CsvManager.cs:35 force-adds Host_IP as column 0 then adds remaining headers with no dedup (:38-46), so any exact duplicate (including a later literal "Host_IP", or "port 1"/"port_1" colliding via the space->underscore rewrite at :45) makes DataTable throw DuplicateNameException, which Form1.cs:9239-9242 surfaces raw and aborts the load. Over-long rows are silently truncated at :61-62 (current behavior is even pinned by unit test LoadFromFile_ExtraColumnsInRow_TruncatesToHeaderLength), and the save path (Form1.cs:9272-9325) rewrites the grid over the same file with no warning, making the loss permanent. No caller or guard mitigates either; medium severity is appropriate since the silent-loss path needs a malformed row plus a save-over.

title: HostConnection.Parse silently mangles IPv6 addresses into wrong hosts; explicit port 22 is overridden by ssh-config
existing_state: HostConnection.Parse splits the Host_IP value on ':' and takes parts[0] as the address (Models/HostConnection.cs:45-51). Any IPv6 literal is silently truncated — `2001:db8::1` becomes host "2001" port 22, and `[::1]:2222` becomes host "[" — with no error; the app then attempts an SSH connection to the garbage hostname. This is on real execution paths: the main-form run (Form1.cs:13317, 14201) and scheduled jobs (Services/JobExecutionService.cs:497). It compounds in jobs: TryGetExplicitPortFromHostValue at JobExecutionService.cs:500 treats any ':'-containing Host_IP as having an explicit port, so the per-row `port` column override is also skipped for IPv6 entries. Related defect in the same file: ApplySshConfig only honors the grid port when it equals 22 (`if (Port == 22 && config.Port.HasValue)`, HostConnection.cs:75-77), so a user who deliberately enters `host:22` to pin the standard port gets it silently replaced by a different Port directive from ~/.ssh/config when EnableSshConfig is on.
recommendation: In Parse, first try System.Net.IPAddress.TryParse on the whole string (bare IPv6 -> address, port 22), support bracket syntax `[v6]:port`, and only then fall back to the single-colon host:port split (e.g. treat inputs with more than one ':' and no brackets as a bare IPv6 address). Mirror the same recognition in JobExecutionService.TryGetExplicitPortFromHostValue. For ApplySshConfig, track whether the port was explicitly supplied (e.g. a nullable backing field or a flag set by Parse when ':port' was present) instead of comparing against the default 22.
user_benefit: IPv6-managed fleets currently cannot be targeted at all — entries fail with misleading connect errors against a truncated hostname — and ssh-config users can have a deliberately pinned port silently changed.

evidence.note: Split(':') truncates IPv6 literals to the first hextet; no bracket handling
Port==22 used as 'not explicitly set' sentinel in ssh-config merge
Parse consumed for job hosts; ':' in value also suppresses the port column override
Main-form execution paths parse Host_IP through the same code

verification.notes: Core defects are real and traced: Parse (HostConnection.cs:45-51) truncates IPv6 to the first hextet; scheduled jobs (JobExecutionService.cs:497, no validation on saved job hosts) do attempt SSH to the garbage hostname and TryGetExplicitPortFromHostValue (lines 564-584) suppresses the port-column override when the final hextet is numeric; the Port==22 sentinel in ApplySshConfig (HostConnection.cs:75-77) does let an ssh-config Port directive override a deliberately pinned :22. However, the description materially errs on the main-form path: Form1.cs:13314 guards every main-form run with InputValidator.IsValidHostOrIp, which explicitly rejects all IPv6 forms (InputValidator.cs:76-79), so those rows are silently skipped — never connected to a truncated host — and Form1.cs:14201 is a grid write-back helper, not an execution path. Net effect (IPv6 unusable; misleading connect errors in jobs only) still justifies medium. [updated refs: Models/HostConnection.cs:45-51 and 75-77 accurate; Services/JobExecutionService.cs:494-506 accurate (TryGetExplicitPortFromHostValue at 564-584); Form1.cs:13317 is guarded by IsValidHostOrIp at 13314; Form1.cs:14201 is UpdateHostColumn (non-execution); IPv6 rejection in Utilities/InputValidator.cs:76-79]

title: Terminal normalizer leaks OSC title-sequence payloads (']0;user@host: ~') into captured command output and can break prompt stripping
existing_state: TerminalOutputProcessor.ProcessEscapeSequence handles only ESC s/u and CSI (ESC [) (Utilities/TerminalOutputProcessor.cs:351-393). For OSC sequences (ESC ] 0 ; title BEL — emitted by the default Ubuntu/Debian bash PS1 and many other shells on every prompt render), neither branch matches: the ESC is consumed at Normalize:98-99, then ']0;user@host: ~' falls into the printable default case (:102-108) and is rendered as literal text, while the BEL terminator is silently dropped (:109-110; Sanitize at :16-18 also strips it but keeps the payload). Every consumer of normalized output gets the garbage — SshShellSession command output (Services/SshShellSession.cs:309,413,498,976) and the interactive terminal transcript (Services/Terminal/InteractiveTerminalService.cs:2719 and siblings). Knock-on effect: the leaked payload prefixes the prompt line, so StripTrailingPrompt's exact-match/regex check (TerminalOutputProcessor.cs:284-286) fails — PromptDetector.BuildPromptRegex anchors the prompt at line start with only \s* slack before the anchor (Utilities/PromptDetector.cs:61) — leaving a ']0;user@host: ~user@host:~$' tail line inside per-command output saved to history. Charset designators (ESC ( B) leak the same way.
recommendation: In ProcessEscapeSequence, add an OSC branch: on ESC ']', consume until BEL (0x07) or ST (ESC \) and emit nothing; also consume two-character sequences ESC ( X / ESC ) X (charset designation) and ESC = / ESC > (keypad modes). Add Normalize unit tests using the stock Ubuntu PS1 byte sequence (\x1b]0;user@host: ~\x07user@host:~$).
user_benefit: Clean command output and history for the most common class of Linux targets — no ']0;...' artifacts in saved run results, and prompt stripping keeps working on hosts whose shells set the terminal title.

evidence.note: Only ESC s/u and CSI handled; ESC ] returns startIndex, payload prints as text
BEL terminator silently swallowed by the 'ignore other control characters' default; payload chars are printable and kept
Prompt regex anchored at line start with only \s* slack — an OSC prefix defeats the match
Normalize output feeds command results and real-time UI output

verification.notes: Reproduced empirically by running the actual TerminalOutputProcessor/PromptDetector code: Normalize(Sanitize("\x1b]0;user@host: ~\x07user@host:~$ ")) yields "]0;user@host: ~user@host:~$" (OSC payload leaks, BEL dropped), and ESC ( B leaks as "(B". The trigger is real: no code sets Rebex TerminalName and the Rebex.Terminal DLL's only terminal-name string is "xterm", which is exactly the TERM case where stock Debian/Ubuntu PS1 emits the title sequence. One nuance softens the history impact: initialization usually captures the contaminated line as the prompt literal, so StripTrailingPrompt's exact-match still removes the tail while the title text is unchanged — the "]0;..." tail line lands in saved output only after the title changes (e.g., any cd), though the live output view and interactive transcript show the garbage on every prompt render regardless.

title: 'Comment Selected Lines' inside a command block scalar doesn't disable anything — it mutates what gets sent to remote hosts
existing_state: The context-menu Comment/Uncomment actions (Form1.cs:5827-5835) call a purely textual per-line transform that inserts `#` after the leading indent of every selected line with no YAML structure awareness (UI/ScintillaScriptEditorControl.cs:406-443, TransformSelectedLines at 1579-1631). Inside a `command: |` / `content: |` block scalar, `#` is NOT a YAML comment — it is literal payload. So a user who selects a few command lines inside a send step and clicks "Comment Selected Lines" believes those commands are disabled, but the step still executes and now sends `#show version`-style lines verbatim to every targeted host. On shells that's usually benign; on network appliances (Cisco/FortiGate CLIs where `#` is not a comment leader) the device receives and reacts to garbage input across the whole fleet. The misleading syntax highlighting compounds it: the highlighter colors the `#...` payload line green like a real comment (YamlSshSyntaxHighlighter.cs:87-88, 148-151 — FindCommentStartIndex has no block-scalar state), visually confirming the wrong mental model.
recommendation: Detect block-scalar regions in CommentSelectedLines/UncommentSelectedLines (same region detection as proposed for the hygiene lints in BUG-070, ideally shared). When the selection is inside a payload, either (a) show a status hint and refuse ("these lines are command payload — '#' would be sent to the host"), or (b) offer to comment out the enclosing step instead. Also stop the highlighter from styling `#` as a comment inside block-scalar bodies so the editor doesn't visually lie about it.
user_benefit: Prevents accidentally shipping '#'-prefixed junk lines to an entire host fleet while believing those commands were disabled.
mockup_idea: Side-by-side: a send step with two payload lines '#commented' shown green (current, looks disabled) vs the proposed warning state where the payload lines stay payload-colored and a hint explains '#' will be sent to the host.

evidence.note: CommentSelectedLines/UncommentSelectedLines: blind per-line '#' insert/remove, no YAML context
per-line comment detection with no block-scalar state — payload '#' lines render as comments
context-menu wiring for comment/uncomment

verification.notes: Traced end-to-end: Comment/Uncomment (ScintillaScriptEditorControl.cs:406-443, TransformSelectedLines 1579-1631) is a blind per-line '#' insert, and the YAML send path (SendCommand.cs:57-84 → SshShellSession.ExecuteAsync, _stream.Send at lines 544/581) transmits block-scalar content verbatim with no '#' filtering — the only '#'-skip guard (SshShellSession.cs:678) is in ExecuteBatchAsync, the legacy simple-command path, which actually trains users to expect '#' to disable lines. The highlighter (YamlSshSyntaxHighlighter.cs:87-88, 148-151) is stateless per-line and paints payload '#' lines comment-green as claimed. All cited line numbers are exact; medium severity is appropriate since the mutated line no longer runs the original command remotely (junk input/error noise rather than command execution).

title: YAML hygiene lints flag block-scalar payloads: false tab/duplicate-key warnings on valid scripts
existing_state: The hygiene lints run line-by-line over the whole script with zero block-scalar awareness (ScriptEditorValidationService.cs:259-354 — the loop never tracks `|`/`>` literal blocks). Consequences: (1) any tab inside a `command: |` / `content: |` payload (a Makefile written via writefile, tab-indented heredoc/Python sent via send) draws "Tab indentation detected; use spaces for YAML indentation" plus a second "Mixed indentation" warning on every such line (lines 267-301) — and a user who 'fixes' it corrupts the payload (Makefiles require tabs); (2) repeated `word: value`-shaped lines at the same indent inside a payload (e.g. two `description: ...` lines in a device config block, or YAML/config content written via writefile) trigger "Duplicate key" warnings (lines 304-354) even though the script is valid YAML — the real parser accepts it, only the lint complains. Additionally duplicate detection uses OrdinalIgnoreCase (line 337) although YAML keys are case-sensitive, so distinct keys like `Path:`/`path:` are falsely flagged. EnableYamlHygieneWarnings is on by default (Models/AppConfiguration.cs:182), so these squiggles persist on perfectly valid production scripts and train users to ignore warnings.
recommendation: In BuildYamlHygieneDiagnostics, pre-compute block-scalar regions (a line whose value ends with `|`, `|-`, `|+`, `>` etc. starts a body covering all subsequent lines indented deeper than the key) and skip both lints inside those regions. Switch the duplicate-key HashSet to StringComparer.Ordinal. ~40 lines in ScriptEditorValidationService.cs plus unit cases in SSH_Helper.Tests/Editor.
user_benefit: Warning squiggles only appear on real problems; users stop being told to 'fix' tabs that are part of the payload they're shipping to remote hosts.

evidence.note: tab/mixed-indent lint inspects leading whitespace of every line, including block-scalar bodies
duplicate-key lint matches `key:`-shaped payload lines; case-insensitive comparer at line 337

title: Editor diagnostics delivery from the validation thread lacks handle/disposal guards (latent cross-thread control access and post-dispose crash)
existing_state: ScriptEditorValidationService raises DiagnosticsUpdated on a threadpool continuation (`ConfigureAwait(false)` + invoke, ScriptEditorValidationService.cs:82-87). The control's handler (UI/ScintillaScriptEditorControl.cs:2291-2305) checks only `IsDisposed` and `InvokeRequired`. Two gaps: (1) Pre-handle delivery — `QueueRefreshAndValidation` explicitly requests validation when the handle is NOT yet created (lines 620-625), and JobEditorDialog assigns editor text in its constructor before ShowDialog (JobEditorDialog.cs:222 `PrepopulateFromJob()` -> line 1581). If the debounced result (min 150ms) arrives before handle creation, `InvokeRequired` returns false (documented WinForms behavior when no handle exists) and `SetDiagnostics` -> `ApplyDiagnosticsVisuals` runs on the threadpool thread, where touching `_editor.TextLength`/indicators (lines 2192-2200) forces the Scintilla handle to be created on a non-UI thread — the control is then permanently broken for the real UI thread. (2) Disposal race — the marshaled lambda `BeginInvoke(() => SetDiagnostics(diagnostics))` (line 2300) has no disposal guard inside it, so a callback that lands after the dialog is closed mid-debounce hits disposed Scintilla and throws ObjectDisposedException. The author guarded the exact same pattern in the sibling path (`IsDisposed || _editor.IsDisposed` inside the lambda, lines 628-634) but not here.
recommendation: In ValidationService_DiagnosticsUpdated: bail (or stash the diagnostics for OnHandleCreated) when `!IsHandleCreated`; add the same `IsDisposed || _editor.IsDisposed` check inside the BeginInvoke lambda as QueueRefreshAndValidation already has; optionally wrap the BeginInvoke call in try/catch (ObjectDisposedException, InvalidOperationException). Alternatively suppress the pre-handle RequestValidationOrClear at line 620-625 and re-request on OnHandleCreated.
user_benefit: Eliminates a rare but real crash/corruption window when opening or closing the Job Editor (or main form) while validation of a YAML preset is in flight.

verification.notes: [severity medium -> low] The missing guards are real (no IsHandleCreated check, unguarded BeginInvoke lambda, threadpool event delivery all verified at the cited lines), but both headline failure modes don't hold. (1) Scintilla5.NET forces handle creation on any property access, and the control's own constructor (ApplyTheme, line 210) creates the inner editor's handle on the UI thread before validation can ever be requested — so a pre-handle delivery cannot create the handle on a threadpool thread or "permanently break" the control; the residual risk is a cross-thread direct native call, and the window closes at JobEditorDialog.cs:230 (SetDarkTitleBar forces the form handle ~8 lines after the text assignment), making the >=150-400ms debounced result landing inside it extremely unlikely. title: Flow Canvas layout autosave races preset switches: the previous preset's positions and sticky notes overwrite the newly active preset
existing_state: React debounces layout-autosave by 300ms (FlowCanvas/src/utils/layoutAutosave.ts:14-17) and nothing cancels the pending timer when a new graph loads. On the C# side, ApplyLayoutAutosave resolves the destination preset from `_activePresetName` AT MESSAGE-ARRIVAL TIME with no identity check in the payload (Form1.cs:2419-2424). Switching presets sets `_activePresetName` first and then reloads the canvas (LoadPresetIntoEditor, Form1.cs:2156-2160). So: drag a block (or toggle expand/disable — debugSlice.ts:75-104 also autosaves), switch presets within ~300ms, and the stale autosave lands on the NEW preset — Positions are cleared and replaced with the old preset's node positions (Form1.cs:2433-2443), and layout.Comments is cleared and replaced with the old preset's canvas notes (Form1.cs:2450-2472). Sticky-kind notes live ONLY in CanvasLayoutData, so the new preset's notes are destroyed and the old preset's notes appear on it; because node ids are deterministically `node-{counter}` for every preset, the corrupted positions also pass the Manual-mode structure-hash merge on the next load.
recommendation: Tag the canvas session with the preset identity: when Form1 sends load-graph, include the active preset name (or a session token), have React echo it back on every layout-autosave/set-layout-mode, and have ApplyLayoutAutosave drop payloads whose preset doesn't match `_activePresetName`. Cheaper stopgap: capture `_activePresetName` into a field when LoadCurrentScriptIntoCanvas sends the graph and route autosaves to that captured name instead of the live one.
user_benefit: Manual layouts and canvas sticky notes are user-authored work; a routine preset switch can currently scramble one preset's arrangement and permanently delete its notes with no error.

title: Flow Canvas undo/redo restores only nodes+edges — breakpoint/expanded Sets, the host's pending breakpoints, isDirty, and the persisted layout all desync
existing_state: UndoSnapshot holds nodes and edges only (FlowCanvas/src/stores/slices/undoSlice.ts:7-12); undo/redo swap them wholesale and clear export status, nothing else (undoSlice.ts:46-98 — no Set state, no `sendLayoutAutosave`, and `isDirty` is neither set nor restored). Three resulting desyncs from the one incomplete restore: (1) Phantom debugger state — toggleBreakpoint writes the breakpoints Set + node data.breakpoint + notifies the host (debugSlice.ts:41-56), and toggleExpanded writes the expandedNodes Set + data.expanded (debugSlice.ts:78-91). Make any snapshotted edit, toggle a breakpoint on, then Ctrl+Z: node data reverts (the gutter dot disappears — BaseBlock.tsx:149 renders from data.breakpoint) but the Set AND the host's _pendingBreakpoints still hold the id, so the next run pauses at a block with no visible breakpoint; the mirror case leaves a dot the executor ignores. The expandedNodes desync recreates the render-expanded vs layout-collapsed mismatch class that previously caused block overlap on preset switches. (2) Stale persisted layout — the host's saved layout is only updated by explicit autosave triggers (drag stop App.tsx:176-179, comment edits, expand/disable toggles, settings commits — utils/layoutAutosave.ts:14-23), so after drag + Ctrl+Z the canvas shows the restored arrangement while the host still holds the pre-undo positions; in Manual layout mode the next open merges the stale positions back via the tuple merge (Services/FlowCanvasBridge.cs:5403-5441), silently resurrecting the exact arrangement the user undid (same for undone comment moves/additions). (3) Undoing all changes back to the loaded state still reports the graph dirty.
recommendation: After every undo/redo in undoSlice.ts: rebuild the three Sets (breakpoints/expandedNodes/disabledBlocks) from the restored node data (data.breakpoint/expanded/disabled carry the truth — one source of truth, ~30 lines) and send the host the breakpoint delta so _pendingBreakpoints stays in sync; call the debounced `sendLayoutAutosave()` so the host's persisted layout always reflects the visible graph; and track the snapshot index at load time to clear `isDirty` when undo returns to the loaded state. user_benefit: Undo stops creating phantom debugger state (runs pausing at blocks with no breakpoint mark), Manual-mode users' undone layout experiments stop silently resurrecting on the next open, and the dirty flag stops lying after a full undo.

title: React Flow's default Backspace delete handler is still enabled — a second, snapshot-less delete pipeline that bypasses undo and dirty tracking
existing_state: The app implements Delete/Backspace itself (hooks/useKeyboardShortcuts.ts:84-94) routing through `removeNodes`/`removeEdges`, which push undo snapshots and set isDirty (graphSlice.ts:427-476). But the <ReactFlow> element never sets `deleteKeyCode` (App.tsx:363-396), and the library default is 'Backspace' (node_modules/@xyflow/react/dist/esm/index.mjs:3586), so React Flow's internal delete handler is ALSO live, emitting removals through `onNodesChange`/`onEdgesChange` — paths that push no undo snapshot, and (for node removals) never set isDirty (graphSlice.ts:243-326; the remove branch at :317-323 returns no isDirty). The two pipelines disagree because selection state is tracked twice and only partially synced: `selectedEdgeIds` is only populated by explicit `selectEdge` calls (graphSlice.ts:478-483; `onEdgesChange` at :328-344 ignores edge 'select' changes), and `selectNodes` (used by paste, :629-631) sets the store Set without setting RF's `node.selected` flags. Whenever RF's internal selection has something the store Sets don't (e.g. edges selected via the selection box, or selected-flagged nodes restored by undo), Backspace deletes them through the snapshot-less RF path — un-undoable, and for nodes also not flagged dirty. The asymmetric key handling also means Backspace and Delete behave differently for the same selection.
recommendation: Set `deleteKeyCode={null}` on the <ReactFlow> element in App.tsx so all deletions funnel through the app's own handler, and make that handler read RF's authoritative selection (nodes/edges with `selected === true`) in addition to the store Sets. As defense in depth, set `isDirty: true` in the `onNodesChange` remove branch (graphSlice.ts:317-323) to match `onEdgesChange`.
user_benefit: Eliminates the class of 'I hit Backspace and Ctrl+Z won't bring it back' losses, and makes Delete/Backspace behave identically — deletions of wiring are structural edits to a preset and must always be undoable.

title: F5 and Ctrl+Enter bypass the Flow Canvas toolbar's run gates — untouched presets get their YAML rewritten and marked dirty, and mid-run F5 corrupts live step correlation
existing_state: The toolbar Run/Test Step buttons send `graphChanged: isDirty` and are disabled while `isRunning || exportStatus.hasErrors || !targetHost` (FlowCanvas/src/panels/Toolbar.tsx:65-83, 104, 118). Worse, pressing F5 during a run still executes ApplyFlowCanvasGraph before the `_executionCoordinator.IsRunning` abort (Form1.cs:6682, 12270-12274), rebuilding the four node<->stepPath correlation maps (Form1.cs:6971-6974) the in-flight run's step highlighting depends on, and re-persisting canvas layout mid-run (Form1.cs:7000). title: Flow Canvas timeline grows unbounded with a full, unsanitized variable snapshot per step execution — long loop runs degrade and can freeze the canvas
existing_state: Every `execution-update` with state 'running' appends a timeline entry carrying a complete copy of all script variables (stores/messageBridge.ts:250-262). `addTimelineEntry` has no cap and rebuilds the entire array on every append (stores/slices/timelineSlice.ts:35-42 — O(N) copy per event, O(N squared) over a run), and entries are only cleared at the start of the next run (messageBridge.ts:216-217). Unlike the iteration log — which strips the heavy `_outputwindow`/`_output` keys, truncates values at 2000 chars, and evicts beyond a user-tunable 500-record cap (stores/slices/iterationSlice.ts:12-32, 222-231) — timeline snapshots are raw: variables holding accumulated command output are cloned in full into every entry. A foreach over a large host list executing a few steps per iteration produces thousands of entries, each duplicating the entire (possibly multi-megabyte) variable map on the WebView2 UI thread mid-run. Secondary defect in the same slice: `updateTimelineEntry` patches every open entry matching the nodeId (timelineSlice.ts:44-50), not the most recent one.
recommendation: Reuse iterationSlice's sanitizer for the snapshot stored on each entry, and add a hard cap (e.g. 1000 entries, evict oldest) in `addTimelineEntry` — or capture variables only on a sampled/last-N basis. Switch `updateTimelineEntry` to patch the latest open entry for the node.
user_benefit: Loop-heavy fleet runs are this tool's core use case; today the canvas gets progressively slower during exactly those runs and can become unresponsive, with the cost invisible until it happens.

title: Editing any property of a Flow Canvas container deletes the inline comments inside its branch bodies on export
existing_state: When a container regenerates from the graph instead of round-tripping its snippet, inline comments that lived inside its branch bodies (do:/then:/else:/cases:) are not re-emitted — acknowledged in the code comment at FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1304-1314 ('Task 5b ... intentionally deferred'). Regeneration is triggered broadly: `_forceGraphExport` is set on ALL ancestor containers by any prop edit (per the export-graph-regeneration design), plus snippet-missing, graph-authored branches, structural modification, or any canvas-authored descendant comment (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1309-1314). So changing one field on a foreach silently strips every `# comment` trailing a command inside its body from the saved YAML. Leading/branch comments survive via the comment-node index (FlowCanvasBridge.cs:1154-1225); only branch-body INLINE comments are lost. This overlaps the documented deferred work in docs/superpowers/plans/2026-06-04-flow-canvas-comment-flow.md (Task 5b), so it is a known gap — included here because the trigger (any container prop edit) is a common path and the loss is silent.

title: Missing REBEX_LICENSE_KEY secret produces a successful release whose SSH features are broken at runtime
existing_state: The Rebex license is injected at build time only if the env var is non-empty: SSH_Helper.csproj:13 (`<RebexLicenseKey Condition="'$(REBEX_LICENSE_KEY)' != ''">`) gates the AssemblyMetadata attribute at csproj:45-50. The workflow maps the secret at build-release.yml:60 with no validation that it is actually set — GitHub silently supplies an empty string for a missing/renamed secret, and unconfigured-secret states are easy to hit (fork, repo migration, secret rotation). At runtime, Program.cs:17-40 tries assembly metadata, then a rebex.key file beside the exe (absent in single-file releases), then the user's REBEX_LICENSE_KEY env var (absent on end-user machines), and if all miss it simply proceeds without setting Rebex.Licensing.Key (the `if` at Program.cs:37-40 has no else). title: Scintilla native DLL extraction trusts any existing file forever — one interrupted first run permanently breaks the editor
existing_state: ExtractEmbeddedResource early-returns whenever the destination file exists (Utilities/ScintillaNativeBootstrap.cs:113-118) and writes with a non-atomic FileMode.Create stream (:127-128). If the process is killed or crashes mid-extraction on first launch (or two instances race — the writer uses FileShare.Read, so a second process can also load a half-written DLL), a truncated Scintilla.dll or Lexilla.dll is left under %LocalAppData%\SSH_Helper\scintilla-native\<version>\win-x64, and every subsequent launch reuses it verbatim: the existence check is the only validation. The result is a persistent, opaque native-load failure in the command editor on every run, fixable only by manually deleting a cache directory the user has never heard of. (The version-segmented path only busts the cache on a ScintillaNET package upgrade.)
recommendation: Make the extraction atomic and self-healing: write to a temp file in the same directory and File.Move/Replace it into place, and validate existing files before reuse (cheapest: compare file length against the embedded resource stream length; re-extract on mismatch). Ten lines in ExtractEmbeddedResource.
user_benefit: An interrupted or concurrent first launch can no longer leave the script editor permanently broken with no user-visible remedy.

title: range() ignores the parse result of its step argument — an unparseable step zeroes it and returns null, silently skipping loops
existing_state: Range initializes step to 1 but then calls `TryResolveInt(parts[2], context, out step)` without checking the return value (Services/Scripting/Functions/CollectionFunctions.cs:151-153). TryResolveInt sets its out parameter to 0 before attempting the parse (CollectionFunctions.cs:291-297), so when the third argument is an unset variable or non-numeric — e.g. `range(0, 10, {{stride}})` with stride undefined — step becomes 0 and the function returns null at line 155 instead of either erroring or keeping the default of 1. A foreach over that result resolves null to an empty list and iterates zero times, so the loop body is silently skipped for the whole run.
recommendation: Check the boolean: `if (parts.Count >= 3 && !TryResolveInt(parts[2], context, out step)) return null;` is the minimal honest fix, but better is to treat an unparseable step as an error (consistent with how start/end already return null at lines 148-149 — and ideally all three should fail loudly rather than null out, per BUG-010's philosophy).
user_benefit: A loop that quietly runs zero iterations looks identical to a successful no-op run; fixing the ignored return makes a bad step argument behave deterministically instead of depending on which argument failed to parse.
